title: Things You Do After Gym That Stop Your Muscles From Growing
text:
Track every set with Symmetry for free 👉🏼 https://symmetry.club/go/greengains

The pump you walk out with is mostly fluid, and it fades within the hour. The muscle you keep gets built later, over the next day or two, once you've left the gym. Your workout is only the signal, so the hours after training matter as much as the session itself. Here are six common after-gym habits that quietly undo your work, and the fix for each.

• Racing the clock with your protein: the total for the day matters more than the rush. Aim for about 0.7 g per pound of body weight (around 125 g a day at 180 lb), 30 to 40 g after training, and one more serving before bed if you lift in the evening
• The ice bath: after lifting, a regular shower is all you need. If you love cold plunges, keep them for rest days
• No record of what you lifted: your muscles grow when you beat last week's numbers. Log every set, count only clean full-range reps, keep your main lifts for at least 6 weeks and go up just 5 lb at a time
• Painkillers for soreness: if it's just soreness, move instead. An easy walk, a few light sets, food and sleep. If they're prescribed for an injury or a condition, keep taking them the way your doctor says
• A hard run after lifting: lift first and keep any cardio after it easy. Hard intervals and long runs go at least 6 hours later or on another day. Walking is fine
• Training late and sleeping short: aim for 7 to 9 hours, set an alarm for bedtime, no caffeine after lunch, go stimulant-free if you train at night and skip the big night out after leg day

In a 12-week study, men who sat in cold water for 10 minutes after every session gained less muscle and less strength than men who pedaled easily on a bike. In another, young adults on 1200 mg of ibuprofen a day for 8 weeks grew their thighs about half as much as a group on a tiny dose of aspirin: under 4% against 7.5%. Five nights of only 4 hours in bed cut muscle building by about a fifth in men who didn't exercise, and about 12 drinks after a hard session cut it by around a quarter, even with protein. And a review of 43 studies found that adding cardio to lifting didn't reduce muscle growth; what it cost was explosive power, most of all in the same session.

The check: pick three main lifts and write down today's numbers. Compare them in 6 weeks. Strength isn't the same as size, but if your lifts haven't moved, your muscles probably haven't either.

Sources & Studies: https://rentry.co/fvu45w2s

title: AI Reveals What 20 Push Ups a Day REALLY Does to Your Body
text:
Download Symmetry and start doing 20 push ups:
👉🏼 https://symmetry.club/go/greengains

Twenty push-ups a day. Less than a minute, on any floor. Does it actually do anything? We put it under the scan, from the first rep to ten years down the road, and look at what the studies found it does to your chest, your arms, your shoulders and your heart, what it doesn't do, and the one thing that decides if your twenty still work after the first month.

• Rep 1: a force plate study measured it. In a regular push-up your hands carry about 64% of your body weight, around 115 lb at 180 lb. Your chest and triceps do most of the pushing, and a small extra push at the top, the push-up plus, makes the serratus work hardest of all
• Set 1: the last hard reps recruit your largest muscle fibres, the ones with the most room to grow. If rep twenty is a real effort, twenty is a good number for you
• The next morning: the soreness comes from tiny damage in the muscle, mostly in the lowering half of each rep. Do them again and it drops sharply
• Week 2: most of the new strength comes from your nervous system. Muscle growth only takes the lead after three to five weeks
• Week 4: push-ups and the bench press both made young men stronger on the bench in four weeks, but muscle thickness didn't change significantly in either group
• Week 8: in a Japanese study, push-ups to failure grew the chest about 20% and the triceps about 10% in eight weeks, as much as the bench press group, and their bench went up about 7 lb without touching a bar
• One year: that's over 7,000 push-ups. If you kept doing the same easy twenty, your body adapted months ago. If you kept making them harder, the gains keep coming, just slower. Bonus: in a big review of exercise trials, regular strength training lowered resting blood pressure by about 4 points
• Ten years: firefighters who could do over 40 push-ups had 96% fewer heart events than men stuck under 10. It's a link, not proof. The benefit of strength training peaked at about 30 to 60 minutes a week, so twenty push-ups are a great start, not the whole plan
• Is twenty the right number? No study has tested twenty a day. For a beginner it might be ten on your knees. For someone fit, twenty regular ones might be a warm-up

Sources & Studies: https://rentry.co/7rso9in2

The plan: push-ups build muscle when the last reps are a real fight, not because of the number twenty. When twenty gets easy, don't jump to a hundred. Make each rep heavier: hands on a 2-foot box (about 40% of your body weight), on your knees (about 50%), a regular push-up (about 64%), feet up 1 foot (about 70%), feet up 2 feet (about 74%). Then lower for three seconds and pause at the bottom. When you can do twenty clean reps on one step, move up to the next, and add rows and squats for your back and legs. How many push-ups can you do in a row right now? Tell me in the comments.

title: AI Reveals What 200g of Protein a Day REALLY Does to Your Body
text:
Download Symmetry to log every set: 👉🏼 https://symmetry.club/go/greengains

Two hundred grams of protein a day is about four big chicken breasts, or more than thirty eggs. Some lifters swear by it, others say it wrecks your kidneys or just turns into expensive pee. So we put it under the scan: the first meal, the first day, the next morning, week 2, week 8, one year and thirty years down the road.

• Meal 1: the old rule said your body can only use about 20 grams at once. In a 2023 study, 100 grams kept muscle building for over 12 hours, longer and bigger than 25 grams
• The first day: your body works hard just to process protein, and when people went from 15 to 30% protein they ate about 440 fewer calories a day
• The next morning: more thirst and more trips to the bathroom. Your liver turns the extra nitrogen into urea and your kidneys flush it out, so drink more water
• Week 8: trained lifters ate about 800 extra calories a day, for eight weeks, and didn't gain fat. But it didn't build extra muscle either
• The limit: a review of 49 trials and over 1,800 lifters saw the gains flatten out at about 0.7 grams per pound of body weight a day. Even the top of the range was about 1 gram per pound
• One year: in a small study of 14 young, healthy trained men, blood tests showed no harm to the kidneys, liver or cholesterol. If you already have kidney disease, ask your doctor first
• Thirty years: in over 2,000 people in their seventies, the ones who ate the most protein lost about 40% less lean mass over three years. It's a link, not proof

Your number: take your body weight in pounds and multiply it by 0.7. One gram per pound is the ceiling the studies support. Split it across at least four meals, and train harder every week, because protein only builds what your workout asks for. How many grams of protein do you eat in a day right now? Tell me in the comments.

title: How Tendon Training Transforms The Entire Human Body
text:
Download Symmetry to log every set: 👉🏼 https://symmetry.club/go/greengains

Every pound your muscles pull has to pass through a tendon before a single bone moves. Most programs never train that link on purpose. So Green tried six tendon moves for his knees, groin, chest, arms, shoulders and heels, then asked AI what fourteen weeks would change.

• Spanish squat: in a British study, people in their seventies who trained their legs with weights for 14 weeks got kneecap tendons 65% stiffer and built force about 27% faster
• The wall sit bonus: a review of 270 trials found that holds cut the top blood pressure number by about 8 points, and cardio by about 4.5
• Copenhagen plank: across 652 Norwegian soccer players, the risk of reporting groin problems was 41% lower
• Push-up hold: holds build strength mostly near the angle you train, and they need at least 70% of your max effort
• Curl hold: the move behind the legend of Alexander Zass, the strongman whose fans say he believed his strength lived in his tendons
• Dead hang: in 140,000 adults, each 11 pounds less grip went with a 16% higher risk of death. It's a link, not proof
• Slow heel lower: in a small 1998 study, all 15 people with long-term Achilles pain were back to running after 12 weeks

The plan: all six moves, three days a week, after a short warm-up. Every week, add five seconds or five pounds. Breathe through every hold, and stop at sharp pain. Which of these six moves will break you first? Tell me in the comments.

Sources & Studies: https://rentry.co/tendon-training-pat...

title: 대부분 근육만 키우고, 진짜 힘은 놓칩니다
translatedTitle: Most people only build muscle and miss out on real strength
text:
체격은 평범하고 근육도 크지 않은데,
턱걸이나 리프팅에서 자기 체중을 훨씬 뛰어넘는 괴력을 발휘하는 사람들이 있습니다.
이 차이는 어디서 오는 걸까요?

단도직입적으로 말씀드리면,
신경계가 근육을 얼마나 끌어다 쓰느냐와 함께, 대부분이 놓치는 한 축이 있습니다.
근육의 힘을 뼈로 전달하는 생체 연결고리,
바로 '힘줄(Tendon)'입니다.


영상 속 수치와 주장의 출처

1. 무겁게 하면 올렸다 내렸다 해도 힘줄이 반응한다 / 가볍게 반복하는 운동은 신호가 약하다
Bohm 등, 2015 메타분석. 건강한 성인 대상 27개 연구를 합친 결과입니다.
최대 힘(또는 1RM, 한 번 들 수 있는 최대 무게)의 70% 이상으로 훈련했을 때는 등척성, 동적, 편심성 수축 사이에 힘줄 강성 증가의 유의한 차이가 없었습니다.
70% 미만 훈련에서는 뚜렷한 변화가 확인되지 않았습니다. 다만 이 구간의 훈련 프로그램은 5개로 적습니다.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4532714/

2. 최대 힘의 70% 이상
위 메타분석에서 70%는 훈련 강도를 나누는 기준선입니다.
오란척 등, 2019 체계적 문헌고찰의 초록도 힘줄의 구조와 기능을 바꾸려면 70% 이상의 고강도 수축이 필요하다고 정리합니다.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30580468/

3. 8주 이상 훈련하고, 12주를 넘기면 변화가 조금 더 크다
메타분석에 포함된 연구는 모두 8주 이상 훈련한 결과입니다.
12주 이상 훈련한 쪽이 8~12주 쪽보다 효과가 컸지만, 통계적으로 유의한 차이는 아니었습니다.

4. 근육이 길게 늘어난 상태에서 버티기
오란척 등, 2019 (소수의 연구를 정리한 것입니다).
근육이 더 길게 늘어난 상태에서 한 등척성 훈련이 짧은 상태보다 근비대가 더 컸고, 동적인 운동 수행으로 이어지는 정도도 더 좋았습니다.

5. 아람파치스 연구팀의 실험 (대표 연구 중 하나)
Arampatzis A, 외. J Exp Biol. 2007.
실험군 11명이 한쪽 다리는 가볍게, 다른 쪽 다리는 무겁게 14주 동안 훈련했습니다. 빈도와 운동량은 비슷했습니다.
무겁게 훈련한 쪽 아킬레스건에서만 힘줄 강성이 올랐고, 일부 부위가 두꺼워졌습니다.
저자들은 힘줄에 가해지는 변형의 크기에 역치가 있다고 해석했습니다.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17644689/

6. 5~10분이면 신호가 최대에 도달한다
Baar K, 2017. Sports Med. 리뷰 논문.
사람 인대 세포로 실험실에서 만든 인공 인대를 시험한 결과를 소개합니다. 운동 시작 후 10분 안에 분자 반응이 최대에 도달했고, 부하를 계속 걸자 신호가 꺼졌으며, 세포가 다시 반응하기까지 약 6시간이 걸렸습니다.
사람 몸에서 같은 결과가 확인된 것은 아닙니다. 바 교수는 이 결과를 바탕으로 다른 훈련과 6시간 간격을 두고 10분 미만의 짧은 세션을 권합니다.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5371618/

7. 10~30초 버티면 힘줄이 이완되며 장력이 퍼진다 (응력 이완)
키스 바 교수의 설명이며 아직 가설입니다.
UC 데이비스 소개글에서는 바 교수 연구실이 10~30초씩 정적 자세를 유지하는 등척성 운동(플랭크, 월싯 등)이 힘줄과 인대 부상 회복에 도움이 된다고 설명합니다. 부상 회복 맥락의 설명입니다.
https://basc.biology.ucdavis.edu/node/10921

영상에는 나오지 않지만 더 읽어볼 자료

1. 20초씩 버티는 훈련이 힘줄 강성을 올린다 (같은 연구 그룹의 2001년 연구 두 편)
각 8명, 12주(주 4일), 최대 힘의 70%로 훈련한 연구입니다.
Kubo K, 외. J Appl Physiol. 2001. 20초씩 하루 4세트로 훈련해 힘줄 강성이 67.5에서 106.2 N/mm로 올랐습니다. 근력은 약 34%, 근육 부피는 약 8% 늘었습니다.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11408409/
Kubo K, Kanehisa H, Fukunaga T. J Physiol. 2001;536(Pt 2):649-655. 훈련량을 같게 맞추고 한쪽 다리는 1초씩 50회 3세트, 다른 쪽 다리는 20초씩 4세트로 훈련했습니다. 근력과 근육 부피는 양쪽이 비슷하게 늘었지만, 힘줄 강성은 20초씩 버틴 쪽에서만 증가했습니다.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2278867/

2. 무릎 힘줄 통증에 등척성 운동
Rio E, 외. Br J Sports Med. 2015.
슬개건병증이 있는 배구 선수 6명 대상 무작위 교차 연구입니다. 등척성 수축 운동 직후 한 발 내림 스쿼트 중 통증(0~10점)이 평균 7.0에서 0.17로 줄었고, 45분 뒤까지 유지되었습니다. 목적은 통증 완화이며, 힘줄이 강해졌다는 결과는 아닙니다.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25979840/
Rio 연구 이후 Aalborg 대학 연구진이 등록한 임상시험에는 무릎 60도, 최대 힘의 70%, 45초씩 5세트, 세트 사이 2분이라는 프로토콜이 적혀 있습니다.
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03528746

3. 등척성 훈련의 목적별 권장 (Lum & Barbosa, 2019 서술 리뷰)

All studies included in the meta-analysis presented results from training for 8 weeks or more.

subtitles.plaintext:
There are people with average builds
and modest muscle size who display
superhuman strength in pull-ups or
lifting, far exceeding their own body
weight. Curious about where this
difference comes from? To put it
bluntly, besides how much the nervous
system utilizes the muscles, there is
one key factor that most people miss.
The biological connection that
transmits muscle force to the bone is
the tendon. Tendons respond even to
basic lifting and lowering movements.
However, there is one condition. It
must be sufficiently heavy. Exercises
involving light, repetitive motions may
grow muscles, but they send a weak
signal to the tendons. Even holding a
plank or a bodyweight squat for two or
three minutes fails to strengthen the
tendons. In today’s video, I will
reveal through the latest sports
medicine research why conventional
exercise methods fail to properly
stimulate tendons, and I will provide a
scientific training protocol to boost
your hidden practical strength while
minimizing strain on your joints. First
, there is one biomechanical fact we
must know. No matter how much force the
muscle contraction generates, that
force must pass through the tendon to
pull the bone for it to manifest as
actual movement and strength. Let's see
what happens if your muscles are strong
but your tendons are loose and soft.
Even when the muscle pulls, the tendon
stretches like a rubber band, causing a
delay before the force is transferred
to the bone. Conversely, if the tendon
becomes stiff, the force is transferred
to the bone much faster the moment the
muscle contracts. This is one of the
reasons why your speed and
explosiveness improve even when your
muscle mass hardly increases. So, you
might wonder why your tendons didn't
get as strong as you expected, even
though you worked hard on squats,
push-ups, and dumbbell exercises,
sometimes even going heavy. Hidden here
is an amazing secret of our body and
the most important core principle of
today's video. It is the physical
property known as the viscosity of the
tendon. Think of a dough made by mixing
cornstarch with water. If you punch
this dough quickly, it instantly
hardens like a stone, repelling the
impact from the surface. However, if
you press your finger slowly and
steadily, your finger sinks deep into
the dough. Professor Keith Baar, a
tendon researcher at the University of
California, Davis, explains that
tendons have similar properties.
According to his explanation, when we
perform fast, repetitive movements like
in standard weight training or
bodyweight exercises over one to two
seconds, the fluid inside the tendons
doesn't have time to escape. As a
result, the tendon turns into a hard
shield, deflecting external stimuli. An
even bigger problem is the stress
shielding phenomenon. If you apply
force in a short burst, only the
already thick and sturdy collagen
fibers within the tendon absorb all
that tension, while the cells deeper
inside that are weak or in need of
strengthening are completely shielded
from the stimulus. Your muscles get
pumped and fatigued, but the tendon
cells themselves don't even register
the fact that you've exercised. Let's
look at how to deactivate this shield
and send a mechanical signal to all the
tendon cells to synthesize collagen
immediately and make the tissue firmer.
The answer lies in isometric
contraction, or "holding" exercises,
where you stop moving and maintain
strong tension for a certain period of
time. As you hold the tension for 10 to
30 seconds, the fluid inside the tendon
is gradually pushed out, causing the
stiff fibers to relax microscopically.
This is called stress relaxation. At
this very moment, the outer fibers that
acted as a shield loosen, allowing the
tension to spread evenly to all cells
inside the tendon, finally switching on
the reinforcement process. However, not
just any "holding" will do. To be blunt
, if you can hold a position for more
than a minute, it is no longer tendon
training. That is merely a
low-intensity muscular endurance
exercise that builds up lactic acid and
metabolic waste in the muscles.
According to a year-long experiment by
Arampatzis’s team at Humboldt
University of Berlin and a
meta-analysis of 27 studies from 2015,
there is an absolute threshold for
changing tendon thickness and stiffness
. The tendon only begins to respond
when it is subjected to a heavy
mechanical load equivalent to at least
70%of your maximum voluntary
contraction. The metabolic pain of a
burning sensation in the muscles is a
completely different concept from the
mechanical tension of a heavy load
pulling strongly on joints and tendons.
In addition to this, there is a 2019
systematic review by Oranchuk’s team
that compiled research on isometric
training. We can pinpoint one specific
way we should be holding these
positions. It is that you must hold
them while the muscle is in a
lengthened state. Isometric training
has the characteristic of only
increasing strength around the specific
joint angle where you performed the
hold. However, in this review, holding
at a point where the joints are deeply
flexed and the muscles and tendons are
taut resulted in greater muscle
hypertrophy and better transfer to
dynamic exercise performance. Here is
one more method I recommend. Go beyond
"yielding isometrics," where you simply
hold your body weight, and utilize "
overcoming isometrics," where you push
or pull against an immovable object
with your maximum effort. When you push
or pull an unmoving object with all
your might, the motor cortex of your
brain wakes up and recruits even the
high-threshold motor units that are
usually dormant. This is the most
realistic way to safely draw out over
70 to 80%of your maximum strength, even
at home without equipment. Now, I will
share a five-movement neuromuscular
integration protocol that combines all
these scientific principles and can be
applied immediately in daily life.
Three absolute principles apply to
every movement. One. The holding time
for each set is exactly 25 to 30
seconds. Two, the intensity must be at
a level of 70 to 80%of your maximum
strength. Gradually build up force for
the first 5 seconds, maintain intensity
for the remaining 20 to 25 seconds, and
never hold your breath—keep it short
and continuous. Three. For movements
involving angles, stop at the point
where the muscles and tendons are most
elongated, within a pain-free range. If
you currently have tendon pain, high
blood pressure, or heart disease, speak
with a doctor or physical therapist
before starting. Start the first two
sets at an intensity of 6 to 7 RPE, and
increase it with each set. The first
movement is the Wall Sit, which targets
the tendons in the front of the knee.
Press your back against the wall, place
your feet about one step forward, and
lower yourself until your thighs are
just above parallel to the floor, then
hold. If you feel discomfort in the
front of your knees, you must stop at a
higher position. If you still
experience pain in the front of your
knees despite this, skip this movement.
If 30 seconds with just your body
weight is easy, place a heavy water
bottle or a backpack full of books on
your thighs, or lift one foot to ensure
the load is challenging enough to
complete the 30 seconds. Perform 3 to 4
sets. The second movement is the
Single-Leg Calf Raise Hold, which
targets the Achilles tendon at the back
of the ankle. Stand on the edge of a
step with one foot, raise your heel as
high as possible, then lower it to the
bottom position and hold. You may hold
onto a wall or railing for balance.
Since one foot supports your entire
body weight, the load is not light. If
this is also easy, wear a backpack
filled with books. Perform 3 to 4 sets
per leg. The third movement is the
Towel Isometric Pull, which awakens the
entire posterior chain and core tendons
. It does not matter if you don't have
a heavy barbell at the gym. Stand with
both feet stepping on the center of a
sturdy, non-stretchy towel or yoga
strap. Bend your knees about 45 degrees
, push your hips back, and keep your
spine straight in a neutral position.
With your arms fully extended, grab
both ends of the towel and pull
vertically with all your might, using
your lower body and back as if you are
lifting the entire floor. Because the
towel does not stretch, the maximum
tension is applied to the tendons of
your forearms, lats, hamstrings, and
glutes exactly in proportion to the
force you exert. Pull and hold for 25
seconds at 80%of your maximum strength.
If 80%is hard to gauge, start the first
two sets at 60-70%and increase it
slightly each set. Perform a total of
four sets. The fourth movement is the
wall push, targeting the tendons in the
chest and front of the shoulders. It
uses the overcoming isometric method I
mentioned, which involves pushing
against an immovable object. Stand
facing a wall or door frame, step one
foot back for stability, place both
hands at chest height, and bend your
elbows so your hands are by your chest.
From that position, push against the
wall for 25 seconds as if you are
trying to push it away. Since the wall
doesn't move, the force you exert
becomes the resistance. If you feel
aching or pinching in the front of your
shoulder, stop immediately and relax
your arms. Repeat for 3 to 4 sets. The
fifth movement is the active hang hold,
which maximizes joint stability for the
upper body pulling chain. Hang from a
bar, but instead of hanging loosely
like a dead hang, pull your shoulder
blades down firmly and hold for 30
seconds while keeping tension from your
forearms to your rotator cuff tendons.
If 30 seconds is easy, add weight to
your waist; if you can't reach 30
seconds, perform a semi-hang by lightly
supporting your feet on the ground.
Repeat for 3 to 4 sets. As a side note,
hanging is one of the videos that
received the most thank-you messages
and the best feedback out of all my
videos. Correcting a slouched posture
helps you regain hidden height, and
gravity pulls your vertebrae apart,
widening the compressed disc spaces and
reducing pressure. This spinal traction
effect is a great help for relieving
and preventing lower back pain.
Furthermore, hanging acts as a form of
self-traction therapy, making it
beneficial for those with disc
conditions or chronic lower back pain.
Also, Dr. John Kirsch, an American
orthopedic surgeon, claimed that the
act of hanging from a bar alone can
heal most shoulder pain. He reported
that after prescribing hanging
exercises to patients advised to have
surgery for shoulder impingement or
rotator cuff injuries, over 90%saw
their pain disappear and no longer
needed surgery. Supporting your entire
body weight with your hands also gives
you the bonus of increased grip
strength. So, it's a good idea to
create an environment in your daily
life to hang consistently. If you
install a doorway pull-up bar at home,
you can hang for a few seconds whenever
you have time. Try to make it a habit
to hang briefly at work by using a
sturdy door frame or a pull-up bar at a
nearby park. However, there are some
precautions to keep in mind when
choosing a doorway pull-up bar. The
grip shouldn't be sparse; it's better
if it’s fully covered. It should also
have a built-in level so you can hang
with proper posture. Since you're doing
this for posture correction, if the bar
is crooked, your body will be too. You
can find information about the
doorframe pull-up bar, which is safe
even for three adults to hang from, in
the pinned comment. For all five
movements, rest for 1 to 2 minutes
between sets. If you don't rest, your
strength will drop below 70%from the
second set onward. Try this protocol
right after your main workout or by
setting aside a separate time.
Excluding rest periods, the total time
of actual tension on your tendons is
just over 10 minutes. According to
Professor Keith Baar's research, the
signal for collagen synthesis in
tendons reaches its peak with just 5 to
10 minutes of stimulation, so there's
no need to hang for tens of minutes.
However, there is one rule of time you
must keep in mind. During the first 2
to 4 weeks after starting this training
, your strength and endurance will
increase very rapidly. This is not
because the tendons themselves have
thickened, but because your brain and
nervous system have become more
efficient at recruiting muscles. It
takes time for tendon tissue, which has
a low blood supply, to actually
rearrange its collagen structure and
achieve physical stiffness. The studies
included in the meta-analysis I
mentioned earlier were all based on at
least 8 weeks of training, and those
exceeding 12 weeks showed even greater
changes. Just because your pain
disappears and you feel stronger in 2
to 3 weeks, don't rush to add weight;
apply tension consistently for exactly
12 weeks. Your joints and functional
strength three months from now will be
on a completely different level than
they are today. If you haven't
subscribed yet, please hit subscribe,
and if you found this video helpful,
please like it and leave a hype comment
.

link, and a weak one. It doesn't prove
fasting hurt anyone,
but it's a good reminder. Nobody has a
long-term trial showing 16-8 makes you
live longer either.
So here's how Green fixed it and what I
do.
One, the window doesn' build anything.
Protein does. Aim for about 0.7 to 1 g
per pound of body weight every day.
Two, split it into at least three
feedings inside your 8 hours. Remember
the muscle full effect.
In one study, after a leg workout, four
feedings of 20 g every 3 hours beat two
big ones and eight small ones for muscle
building.
So on 16:8, think noon, 4 and 8. A meal,
a shake, a meal.
Three, train inside the window or right
before it opens so your first meal lands
after your session.
Four, watch your lifts, not just the
scale. Green moved his workout to 11:30,
ate at noon, 4 and 8 and doubled his
protein. Four weeks later, 70s for 8
again, then the 75s.
Same 16 hours, completely different
result.
So what's your window right now? 16:8,
18:6 or breakfast at 7 like a normal
human? Tell me in the comments.
And remember to download Symmetry to
know if your fast is burning fat or your
muscle. Now go grow.

title: 5 Killer Dumbbell Exercises for Bigger, Rounder Shoulders
text:
Download Symmetry to grow your shoulders 👉🏼 https://symmetry.club/go/greengains

A round shoulder has three parts: the front, the side and the back. These 5 dumbbell exercises hit all three, with the form that studies found makes your delts do more of the work, and the one rule that decides whether any of it grows. All you need is a pair of dumbbells and a bench.

• Lateral raise (side): raise your arms to shoulder height, not higher, and keep them almost straight. In men, the side delt worked hardest with a straight arm, and less and less as the elbow bent
• Standing dumbbell press (front + side): of four ways to press, standing with dumbbells made the delts work the hardest. Sitting down cut the side delt by about 15%. If you have to lean back, go lighter
• Wide-grip upright row (side + upper traps): the wider the grip, the harder the side delts and traps worked, and the less the biceps helped. Elbows up to shoulder height
• Bent-over rear delt fly (back): in a computer model, this fly asked about a fifth more of the rear delt than a bent-over row. Palms facing in, thumbs up
• Chest-supported rear delt row (back + upper back): elbows flared wide, upper arms level with your shoulders. Tuck them in and it turns into a regular back row

The rule: work in 8 to 12 reps. Once you get all 12 with clean form, grab a heavier pair, even if it drops you back to 8. In a 2026 study, the arm that kept moving up in weight grew about twice as much as the arm that kept the same weight. If the next dumbbell is too big a jump, add a rep instead.

The plan: twice a week, 3 sets of each, with the press first while you're fresh. Which of these 5 are you skipping right now? Tell me in the comments.

Sources & Studies: https://rentry.co/xuxffhv2

turns testosterone into estrogen. The
more fat gorilla carries, the more
aromatase gets made, and the more
testosterone gets converted away. More
fat, more estrogen, less testosterone,
more fat. A cycle that just keeps
feeding itself. So, what does gorilla
do? Gorilla, stay between 12% and 15%
body fat. If gorilla go below 8%,
hormones crash, constant fatigue
imbalance. And if gorilla go above 20%,

whole food. Testosterone is made from
cholesterol. So gorilla eats enough
healthy fats, eggs, red meat, avocado,
olive oil, and fatty fish like salmon,
tuna. That's the raw material
testosterone actually gets built from.
Four, gorilla controls stress. Cortisol
isn't bad by itself. It helps gorilla
survive stress, keep blood sugar steady.
But when cortisol stays high from poor
sleep, overtraining, or doom scrolling
at 2:00 a.m., it becomes testosterone's
enemy. High cortisol raises blood sugar,
builds belly fat, and drops testosterone
even more. Gorilla cuts alcohol, keeps
stress low, and protects his sleep.
Cortisol drops, testosterone rises. So
here's the whole jungle plan. Sleep 7 to
9 hours, lift heavy compound lifts, sit
between 12% and 15% body fat, eat real
fats and real protein, cut the alcohol,
cut the stress, cut the 2:00 a.m.
scrolling. No gummy did that, no powder
did that, gorilla did that. Weeks go by.
Gorilla wakes up again, checks the
mirror. Same gorilla, except this time
the battery's full, the fire's back, and
gorilla's actually got a reason to smile
at himself. That's not luck, that's just
gorilla finally training the hormone
instead of guessing at it. Now go boost
it.

Number five, it lets you squeeze out

Here's a mechanism that explains why

brain isn't actually a separate system
running on entirely different rules.
It's tapping into the exact same energy
pathway your muscles depend on. It's
genuinely fascinating when you think
about how energy-hungry your brain
actually is relative to its size.
Despite making up only a small
percentage of your total body weight,
your brain consumes a surprisingly large
share of your body's total daily energy
expenditure, which makes it a lot less
surprising that a compound supporting
rapid cellular energy availability might
have effects reaching beyond just muscle

Number seven, any extra beyond what your
muscles can store gets filtered out as

Your body simply isn't capable of

consistency matters so much more than
precise timing around your workouts.

and slightly depleting their creatine

dose delivering some lasting permanent
effect. Understanding this mechanism
explains why sporadic or inconsistent
use delivers such underwhelming results
compared to steady daily intake. You're
essentially trying to keep a reservoir
topped off, and skipping days repeatedly
just means that reservoir gradually
drains back down before you get the
chance to build it back up again. It's a
bit like watering a plant. Missing a
single day rarely causes any noticeable
harm, but a consistent pattern of
forgetting means that plant never
actually gets the chance to reach and
maintain its full healthy potential over
time. So, let's zoom out for a moment
and connect all eight of these
mechanisms into one single coherent
picture. Creatine works by topping off a
natural energy storage system your body
already runs, giving your muscles a
bigger emergency reserve for short

train with slightly more total volume
over time, extending that same energy
benefit to your brain, filtering out
anything beyond what your muscles can
actually use, and requiring consistent
daily intake to keep that whole system
running at its full potential. None of
these individual mechanisms sound
particularly dramatic on their own, and
that's honestly the whole point.
Creatine doesn't work through flashy
single dramatic effect. It works through
a handful of small interconnected
biological processes that compound
together gradually over weeks and months
of consistent use.
Understanding this actually makes the
supplement feel a lot less mysterious
and a lot more like exactly what it is,
a well-understood, well-researched tool
that does something genuinely useful,
just quietly and gradually, rather than
instantly and dramatically. If there's
one common thread connecting all eight
of these mechanisms together, it's that
creatine consistently works by
supporting and amplifying processes your
body is already running, rather than
introducing some entirely foreign,
dramatic new function. That's honestly a
big part of why it has such a strong,
long-standing safety record. It's not
fighting against your body's natural
biology, it's simply giving an existing,
well-established system a bit more raw
material to work with over time. So,
there you have it. Eight things creatine
actually does inside your body,
explained in a way that hopefully makes
this entire topic feel a lot less
mysterious than it did 5 minutes ago.
The overall takeaway here is pretty
simple once you understand the
mechanism. Creatine isn't magic, it's
just really well-understood biology,
quietly topping off a system your body
was already running, one consistent
daily scoop at a time. If you've been
taking creatine for a while without ever
really understanding what was happening
beneath the surface, hopefully this
gives you a a clearer sense of why the
timing debates matter less than people
think, why patience genuinely pays off,
and why that first couple weeks of
feeling a little fuller isn't something
to worry about. It's simply your biology
doing exactly what it's designed to do.
Now, I want to hear from you. Which of
these eight mechanisms genuinely
surprised you the most, or which one
finally made something about your own
experience with creatine click into
place? Maybe you've been taking it for
years and never actually understood why
it worked until watching this video. Or
maybe you're still on the fence, and
this finally gave you the clarity you
needed to decide. Drop a comment down
below because I genuinely love hearing
which parts of the science resonate most
with different people. And if this video
helped you actually understand what's
happening every time you take that daily
scoop, do me a favor and smash that like
button, subscribe if you're new here,
and I'll see you in the next one.
Stay curious, stay consistent, keep
learning the why behind the habit, and
I'll catch you soon.

short-duration activities like heavy

gives up a phosphate molecule to power a
muscle contraction, it becomes exhausted
adenosine diphosphate or ADP, leaving
your muscles fatigued and unable to
contract with high force. This is where
daily creatine saturation pays massive
dividends. Phosphocreatine instantly
donates its high-energy phosphate group
back to ADP, rapidly converting it back
into usable, high-energy ATP right
inside the muscle fiber. Taking 5 g
daily ensures this biochemical
conversion process happens at lightning
speed, allowing you to maintain peak
power output, delay localized muscular
fatigue, and sustain high force
production during demanding workouts.
Over time, those extra reps and
high-energy seconds compound into
significantly greater strength gains and
overall athletic performance. This rapid
energy turnover fundamentally changes
how your body handles intense physical
work. When performing heavy squats,
deadlifts, or bench presses, the
limiting factor is rarely your
willpower. It is the sudden depletion of
immediate cellular energy. By
accelerating ATP resynthesis, daily
creatine allows you to maintain a higher
bar speed and produce greater force late
into your sets. Rather than experiencing
a steep, cliff-edge drop-off in
performance after rep three or four, you
gain the physiological capacity to
sustain output through reps six, seven,
or eight. This elevated work capacity
provides a superior mechanical stimulus
to your muscle fibers, forcing them to
adapt and grow stronger than they ever
would under normal, non-supplemented
energy conditions. Number three,
intracellular water retention causes
muscles to look fuller.
Have you ever stepped on the scale after
a week or two of daily creatine and
wondered why your body weight suddenly
jumped by two to four pounds? When
creatine molecules are transported into
your muscle cells via specialized
transporter proteins, they naturally
draw water along with them through a
well-documented process known as
cellular hydration or osmosis.
It is crucial to understand that this is
intracellular water retention, meaning
the water is pulled directly inside the
muscle cells, rather than sitting under
your skin as soft, bloated subcutaneous
fluid. This subtle increase in muscle
cell volume physically expands the
muscle tissue from within, giving your
physique a noticeably fuller, harder,
and more dense appearance almost
overnight.
Beyond basic aesthetics, this expanded
cell volume creates a physical pressure
state inside the cell wall, which acts
as a powerful anabolic signal that
stimulates further muscle protein
synthesis. Many people panic when they
see the scale move upward during their
first few weeks on creatine, assuming
they have somehow gained unwanted body
fat. However, medical and sports science
research clearly confirms that this
early weight gain is almost entirely
composed of clean intracellular water
stored directly within your skeletal
muscle tissue. Well-hydrated muscle
cells are far more resilient to
mechanical strain, exhibit better
nutrient transport across the cell
membrane, and maintain a superior
environment for biological repair.
Furthermore, this intracellular
hydration state plays a vital role in
protecting your muscles against heat
stress and dehydration during intense
workouts, keeping cellular temperature
stabilized while you train. Number four,
lean muscle mass production accelerates
over time. What if a daily supplement
could directly trigger the key genetic
signals responsible for building new,
lasting lean muscle mass? While creatine
itself is not an amino acid or a
structural protein, taking 5g daily
creates an environment that drastically
speeds up muscle hypertrophy when paired
with resistance training. The
combination of increased cellular
hydration, higher workload capacity in
the gym, and elevated total training
volume triggers essential cellular
growth pathways like the mTOR pathway,
which directly regulates cell growth and
protein synthesis.
Additionally, long-term daily creatine
supplementation has been shown to down
regulate levels of myostatin, a
regulatory protein in your body that
naturally acts as a cap or break on
muscle growth.
By gently lowering myostatin activity
and increasing the activation of
myogenic satellite cells, daily creatine
helps your body build and repair muscle
tissue far more effectively after every
workout. The mechanical advantage
provided by daily creatine
supplementation creates a powerful
cascade of muscle-building events.
Because you can lift heavier weights,
perform more reps, and recover faster
between sets, you place significantly
greater mechanical tension on your
muscle fibers during every workout.
Mechanical tension is widely regarded as
the primary driver of muscle
hypertrophy.
Over weeks and months, this extra
training stimulus forces your body to
adapt by synthesizing new contractile
proteins. Therefore, the physical muscle
tissue you build while supplementing
with creatine is real, permanent muscle
mass, not just temporary water weight.
Number five, fatigue resistance and
workout recovery. Picture finishing a
brutal workout and feeling energized and
ready to tackle your day, rather than
collapsing in total exhaustion. Daily
creatine intake helps buffer the
accumulation of hydrogen ions and
metabolic waste products that cause that
familiar burning sensation during
intense exercise. Because your energy
systems operate with maximum efficiency,
your muscles undergo less acute
metabolic stress for the exact same
amount of work performed.
Furthermore, clinical research indicates
that taking 5 g of creatine daily
reduces markers of cellular damage, such
as creatine kinase and lactate
dehydrogenase, following high-volume
training sessions. By reducing muscle
cell breakdown and supporting rapid
glycogen replenishment when taken
alongside carbohydrates, your body
bounces back much faster between workout
days, allowing you to train with
consistent intensity week after week.
Recovery is where true fitness progress
actually happens, and daily creatine
accelerates this process on multiple
fronts.
After a challenging training session,
your muscle glycogen stores are depleted
and your muscle membranes experience
micro tears. Supplementing with 5 g of
creatine daily enhances muscle glycogen
resynthesis when consumed with
post-workout carbohydrates, helping your
muscles reload their primary energy fuel
far faster than they would on food
alone. In addition, creatine plays a
vital role in reducing central nervous
system fatigue. When cellular energy is
abundant throughout your neuromuscular
system, neural fatigue is significantly
muted, keeping your energy levels high
and your daily motivation rock solid
throughout your training blocks. Number
six, cognitive function and mental
energy receive a boost.
Did you know that your brain consumes
roughly 20% of your body's total resting
energy despite accounting for only about
2% of your overall body weight? Just
like your skeletal muscles, your brain
relies heavily on ATP and
phosphocreatine to power complex
cognitive tasks, maintain sharp focus,
and process information under pressure.
Taking 5 g of creatine daily increases
brain phosphocreatine levels by up to
10%, providing your neurons with a
steady accessible reservoir of rapid
energy. Extensive scientific studies
show that daily creatine supplementation
noticeably improves working memory,
processing speed, and mental clarity,
particularly during periods of sleep
deprivation, intense mental fatigue, or
demanding cognitive workloads.
For individuals who do not consume red
meat, such as vegetarians and vegans,
the cognitive benefits of daily creatine
are often even more pronounced.
Think of your brain as a
high-performance supercomputer that
constantly demands immediate power. When
faced with complex problem-solving or
prolonged focus during a stressful work
day, your neurons consume ATP at an
accelerated rate.
When local brain creatine stores are
fully saturated, your brain cells can
rapidly resynthesize ATP, preventing
sudden brain fog and cognitive drop-offs
during demanding tasks. By supporting
steady cellular energy production within
key brain regions like the prefrontal
cortex, daily creatine helps buffer
against mental exhaustion, keeping your
focus sharp, your mind calm, and your
cognitive processing smooth, even when
life gets hectic. Number seven,
neuroprotective and longevity pathways
are activated. What if the most
important long-term benefit of daily
creatine has nothing to do with how much
weight you can bench press, but how well
your brain and nervous system age over
the next several decades?
Emerging cutting-edge scientific
research suggests that consistent daily
creatine intake exerts powerful
neuroprotective effects across the
central nervous system. By supporting
cellular bioenergetics and reducing
oxidative stress inside neuronal
mitochondria, creatine helps protect
delicate brain cells against metabolic
dysfunction, excitotoxicity, and
cellular decay.
Researchers are actively investigating
creatine's therapeutic potential in
mitigating age-related cognitive
decline, supporting recovery from mild
traumatic brain injuries or concussions,
and offering protective benefits against
neurodegenerative conditions. This
metabolic shield positions 5G daily as a
legitimate longevity molecule for
long-term health span and nervous system
resilience. As we age, mitochondrial
efficiency naturally declines across all
tissues, with the brain being
particularly vulnerable to this decrease
in cellular energy production. When
neuronal mitochondria struggle to
produce adequate ATP, cellular damage
accumulates, leading to cognitive
slowing.
Daily creatine supplementation acts as a
vital metabolic backstop.
By maintaining elevated phosphocreatine
availability directly within brain
tissue, creatine preserves mitochondrial
function and reduces the generation of
harmful reactive oxygen species,
ensuring your neurons can withstand
metabolic stress far better over time.
Number eight, bone mineral density and
structural integrity support grows.
What if taking a daily supplement could
help keep your skeletal system dense,
strong, and resistant to fractures as
you age.
While creatine is primarily celebrated
for its muscular and neurological
effects, your bones are dynamic, living
tissues that constantly respond to
mechanical strain and cellular energy
availability.
When you take 5 g of creatine daily
while engaging in regular strength
training, the increased muscular force
output exerts greater mechanical load on
your bones, stimulating osteoblast
activity, the specialized cells
responsible for synthesizing new bone
matrix. Furthermore, osteoblasts
themselves require significant ATP to
produce collagen and mineralized bone
tissue. By supplying bone cells with
enhanced energy reserves, daily creatine
helps slow down age-related bone mineral
density loss, offering a dual action
defense against sarcopenia and
osteoporosis as you grow older. Bone
tissue does not grow stronger in a
vacuum. It responds directly to the
physical pull exerted by contracting
skeletal muscles. Because daily creatine
supplementation allows you to lift
heavier weights and generate higher peak
muscular forces, your bones receive a
far stronger osteogenic stimulus during
every workout.
Over time, this mechanical signal tells
your body to deposit more calcium into
the bone matrix, increasing structural
density in key areas like the hips and
spine. This skeletal support is
particularly revolutionary for aging
adults, offering a comprehensive,
full-body solution for maintaining
physical independence and structural
integrity throughout your lifespan.
Number nine, minor initial digestive
disturbance can occur.
Have you ever experienced a mild upset
stomach or light bloating shortly after
starting a new daily supplement routine?
While 5 g of creatine daily is
overwhelmingly safe and exceptionally
well tolerated by the vast majority of
human beings, taking it without enough
liquid or on a completely empty stomach
can occasionally cause light
gastrointestinal discomfort.
Because creatine is an osmotically
active compound, it naturally draws
fluid into the stomach and intestinal
tract before it is fully absorbed into
your bloodstream. Taking a full 5 G dose
all at once with just a small sip of
water can cause transient cramping or
loose stools in sensitive individuals.
Fortunately, this minor issue is
completely avoidable. Simply mixing your
daily 5 G with 12 to 16 oz of water,
taking it alongside a solid meal, or
splitting the dose into two smaller 2.5
G servings will keep your digestive
system completely happy while
maintaining maximum absorption.
Using micronized creatine monohydrate
can eliminate digestive sensitivity
altogether.
Micronized creatine has been processed
to reduce the particle size of the
powder by up to 20 times, vastly
increasing its surface area and
solubility in water.
This finer powder dissolves
effortlessly, passes through the stomach
quickly, and enters circulation without
causing fluid pooling in the digestive
tract. By adopting these simple habits,
you can completely sidestep any
digestive friction and enjoy the
physical and cognitive benefits of daily
creatine with total comfort. Number 10,
your natural creatine production pauses
temporarily without downside.
What happens to your body's internal
production line when you supply it with
5 g of pure creatine every single day
from an external source?
Under normal dietary conditions, your
liver and kidneys endogenously
synthesize around 1 to 2 g of creatine
per day from precursor amino acids. When
you take 5 G daily via supplementation,
your body recognizes the abundant
external supply and temporarily down
regulates its endogenous production to
conserve metabolic energy and raw
materials. However, unlike synthetic
hormones, this natural down regulation
is entirely harmless, self-regulating,
and fully reversible. If you ever decide
to pause or stop taking daily creatine,
your liver and kidneys will smoothly
resume their natural baseline production
within a few weeks with zero long-term
damage, organ strain, or permanent
suppression of your metabolic systems.
Decades of rigorous clinical research
confirm that long-term creatine use does
not compromise renal function or hepatic
health in healthy individuals.
Blood tests may show a slight elevation
in serum creatinine levels, but serum
creatinine is simply a harmless
metabolic breakdown product of stored
creatine.
In a person supplementing with daily
creatine, higher blood creatine is an
expected harmless marker of elevated
muscle creatine stores, not a sign of
kidney dysfunction.
Once you stop taking the supplement,
serum creatinine levels naturally return
to baseline alongside the restoration of
your body's internal production.
When you step back and examine the full
physiological picture, taking 5 g of
creatine monohydrate every single day
emerges as one of the most effective,
safe, and transformative habits you can
build for your physical and mental
health.
From saturating your muscle
phosphocreatine stores and rapidly
resynthesizing ATP during intense
exertion to enhancing intracellular
muscle volume, accelerating muscle
hypertrophy, and boosting athletic
recovery, the physical advantages are
unmatched.
Simultaneously, the profound cognitive
benefits, including sharper working
memory, mental fatigue resistance,
neuroprotection, and long-term bone
density support, make 5 g of daily
creatine a true full-body longevity
supplement for people of all ages and
fitness levels. Now that you know the
exact physiological transformation that
happens when you take 5 g of creatine
every single day, now I want to hear
from you. Have you already added daily
creatine to your routine, or were you
holding back because of water weight
myths and safety concerns? Drop your
experiences, questions, and daily
results in the comments down below. And
if you enjoyed this science-backed
breakdown, make sure to hit that like

I'll catch you in the next video.

extra water where it actually helps.
Athletes and researchers call this cell
volumization, and it's actually one of
the reasons your muscles start looking a
little fuller, rounder, and more defined
pretty quickly, sometimes within the
first couple weeks. So, if you weigh
yourself and freak out because the
number jumped, relax. Your body isn't
failing you, it's just storing a little
extra water exactly where you want it,
inside the muscle tissue itself, not
sitting under the skin making you look
puffy. Most people find this initial
jump levels off after the first couple
weeks, and from there, the scale tends
to move much more gradually in line with
actual training progress rather than
this quick initial spike. Change number
two, your strength numbers start
creeping up faster than normal. Have you
ever hit a frustrating plateau where
your bench press just wouldn't budge no
matter how hard you tried, no matter how
many different programs you followed?
This is usually where creatine quietly
starts doing its best, most underrated
work behind the scenes. See, creatine's
main job in your body is to help
regenerate a molecule called ATP, which
is basically your muscle's immediate
energy currency for short explosive
efforts, think heavy lifts, sprints,
jumps, anything that demands a quick,
powerful burst rather than steady
endurance.
With more creatine stored in your
muscles, your body can regenerate ATP
faster during those short bursts, which
means you can often squeeze out one or
two extra reps you simply couldn't
manage before, even on days you feel a
little tired.
Multiply that across weeks and months
and even years of consistent, dedicated
training, and that's how people end up
with noticeably better strength gains
compared to lifters who aren't
supplementing at all.
It's not magic, and it's definitely not
an overnight transformation. It's just
giving your muscles a bigger fuel tank
for short, intense effort, which
compounds nicely over time. Researchers
have documented this effect across a
wide range of training styles, from
powerlifting to sprinting to general
resistance training, which is part of
why creatine remains one of the few
supplements that nearly every strength
coach agrees actually works. Change
number three, your muscles start
recovering a little quicker between
sets. Ever notice how some people seem
completely ready to go again after 90
seconds while you're still gasping for
air, hands on your knees, questioning
your life choices?
Part of that comes down to how
efficiently your body replenishes ATP
between efforts, and creatine directly
speeds that process up in a measurable
way.
When your ATP stores get replenished
faster between sets, you're not just
stronger in the moment, you're able to
maintain higher output set after set
instead of your performance dropping off
a cliff by set three or four like it
normally would. This is one of those
changes that doesn't necessarily show up
on a scale or in a mirror, and nobody's
going to compliment you on it at the
gym, but if you're tracking your
workouts closely, you'll start to notice
you're simply not falling apart as fast
during a session.
It's a small edge on paper, but across
dozens of workouts, that edge adds up
into something real, especially if your
training involves multiple sets of
compound lifts where fatigue usually
starts wrecking your form and output by
the later sets.
Think about it this way. If you're
consistently able to maintain better
output on your fourth and fifth sets
instead of coasting through them just to
finish, that's real meaningful volume
you weren't getting before, and it
compounds across an entire training
block.
Change number four, your brain might
actually start working a bit
differently. Wait, creatine affects your
brain, too? Yeah, and this is the part
almost nobody talks about because
everyone instantly associates creatine
purely with the gym, purely with muscles
and lifting heavy things. Turns out your
brain uses a surprisingly large amount
of ATP as well, especially during
periods of mental fatigue, sleep
deprivation, or high stress, all of
which drain your energy reserves fast.
Several studies have found that creatine
supplementation may support cognitive
performance, particularly memory and
processing speed, during conditions
where your brain is under real strain,
like sleep deprivation or intense,
demanding mental tasks that require
sustained focus. It's not going to turn
you into a genius overnight, and the
effect tends to be more noticeable in
vegetarians or people with naturally
lower baseline creatine stores, since
they're not getting much from diet
alone, but it's a legitimately
interesting and still expanding area of
research worth keeping an eye on,
especially as more universities start
dedicating entire research programs
specifically to how creatine interacts
with brain energy metabolism. So, if
you've been feeling foggy lately,
running on low sleep, or just mentally
drained from work or school, this might
be one more reason to pay closer
attention to your daily creatine intake,
even on the days you have no plans to
hit the gym at all. Change number five.
You might feel thirstier than usual.
Have you ever started a new supplement
and suddenly felt like you needed water
constantly, almost like your body was
sending you signals you'd never noticed
before?
That's a real and pretty common
experience with creatine, and there's a
simple, logical explanation behind it.
Since creatine draws water into your
muscle cells, your body's overall water
demand increases slightly, and your
thirst signals often adjust accordingly
to compensate for that shift. This is
exactly why most coaches and researchers
recommend bumping up your daily water
intake when you start creatine, not
because it's dangerous if you don't, but
because staying well hydrated helps you
actually get the full benefit of what
creatine is doing at the cellular level,
letting it do its job properly. So,
don't be shocked if your water bottle
empties faster than it used to, or if
you find yourself refilling it more
often throughout the day. Your body's
just asking for what it needs to make
the most of the extra creatine sitting
in your muscles.
A good rule of thumb a lot of coaches
suggest is simply paying attention to
your urine color and drinking whenever
you're thirsty, rather than trying to
hit some arbitrary number of liters you
saw in a random article somewhere, since
everyone's actual hydration needs differ
based on body size, climate, and how
much they sweat during training. Change
number six, that old creatine destroys
your kidneys.
Rumor isn't holding up. You've probably
heard someone say creatine is hard on
your kidneys, maybe even a well-meaning
family member who read it somewhere
years ago, and honestly, it's one of the
most persistent myths in the entire
fitness world. Here's the actual story
behind it. This concern mostly comes
from the fact that creatine
supplementation slightly raises a marker
called creatinine, which doctors
normally use to assess kidney function
during routine blood work. But in people
with healthy kidneys, this rise isn't a
sign of damage at all. It's just a
normal expected byproduct of how
creatine gets metabolized and processed
by the body. Multiple long-term studies,
some running over several years with
regular monitoring, have consistently
found no evidence of kidney harm in
healthy individuals taking standard
doses like 5 g a day.
Obviously, if you already have existing
kidney issues, that's a conversation to
have with a doctor first before starting
anything new. But for the average
healthy person, this fear has been
repeated so often online that people
assume it's proven, settled science,
when it's really just an old myth that
never quite died out. Even major sports
medicine organizations have come out and
stated that creatine is safe for
long-term use in healthy adults, which
is a pretty strong signal if you're
still on the fence about it, especially
considering how cautious those
organizations tend to be before making
any kind of blanket safety statement
about a supplement. Change number seven,
your muscles start holding more fuel
reserve even on rest days. Okay, this is
the one I mentioned earlier, the one
that honestly surprised me the most when
I first learned about it. A lot of
people assume creatine only matters on
the days you actually train hard, but
that's not really how it works
underneath the surface. Creatine builds
up in your muscle tissue gradually over
time, meaning your stores stay elevated
even on your rest days, your travel
days, the days you skip the gym entirely
because life gets busy. This matters
because your muscles are essentially
sitting on a bigger reserve tank at all
times, not just during workouts
themselves, ready to be tapped into
whenever you need it. It's part of why
consistency matters so much more than
timing with creatine, taking it daily,
even on off days when you're not
training at all, keeps your muscle
saturation levels topped off so you're
always walking around with that extra
performance buffer ready to go the
moment you actually need it.
This is also why skipping a few days
here and there isn't the end of the
world, but going weeks without it will
slowly drain those stores back down
toward baseline, undoing a lot of the
progress you built up. Change number
eight, muscle cramps probably aren't
coming from the creatine. Ever hear
someone blame their leg cramps on
creatine and swear they're never
touching the stuff again? This is
another myth that gets repeated
constantly in gym locker rooms and
online forums, but when researchers
actually looked into it directly with
real controlled studies, the data simply
didn't back it up.
Several studies comparing creatine users
to non-users found no meaningful
increase in muscle cramping or
dehydration-related issues between the
two groups.
If anything, some research suggests
better hydration status in muscle tissue
could theoretically help rather than
hurt in this department, which is the
opposite of what most people assume.
Cramps are usually caused by a mix of
things like electrolyte imbalances,
overtraining, poor sleep, or just not
drinking enough water in general
throughout the day, creatine tends to
get unfairly blamed simply because
people notice it happening while they're
also training harder and pushing
themselves more than before, which makes
it an easy scapegoat even when the
timing is really just a coincidence.
Change number nine, your workout volume
might quietly increase over time.
Have Have ever looked back at your
training log after a few months and
realized you're doing way more total
work than when you first started without
even really noticing it happen?
This is one of those slow, sneaky
changes that's easy to miss in the
moment, but obvious in hindsight.
Because creatine helps you push out a
few extra reps per set and recover a bit
faster between sets, your total training
volume, meaning the overall amount of
work you're doing across an entire
session, tends to creep upward steadily
over time, week after week. And total
volume happens to be one of the biggest
drivers of long-term muscle growth that
exists in exercise science. So, it's not
that creatine builds muscle directly by
itself like some magic switch, it's that
it enables you to do more productive
work more consistently over a longer
stretch of time, which is really the
actual engine behind noticeable physique
changes after months of steady training.
It's a quiet, unglamorous kind of
progress, but it's exactly the kind that
shows up in the mirror eventually, even
if you can't point to any single workout
where it clicked. This is honestly why
so many long-term creatine users say the
results feel less like a dramatic
transformation and more like a gradual,
steady climb that only becomes obvious
when you look back at old photos.
Change number 10, your body composition
can shift even if the scale doesn't show
a big change. Ever feel like your body
is clearly changing, your clothes fit
differently, but the scale number just
won't cooperate no matter what you do?
This happens a lot with creatine users
and it makes complete sense once you
understand what's actually going on
beneath the surface. Between the small
amount of water retention pulling your
weight up slightly and gradual muscle
growth from your increased training
capacity over time, the scale can look
almost unchanged for a while, even
though your actual body composition,
more lean tissue, similar or even lower
fat percentage, is genuinely shifting
underneath it all.
This is exactly why a lot of experienced
coaches tell people to stop obsessing
over the scale number specifically and
pay more attention to how their clothes
fit, progress photos taken under the
same lighting, or their actual strength
numbers in the gym instead. The scale,
honestly, is one of the worst tools
available for tracking what creatine is
actually doing to your physique over
time, and leaning on it too heavily can
make you feel discouraged even when
real, meaningful progress is happening
right underneath your skin quietly, week
after week, whether the number on the
scale wants to cooperate with you or
not. So, there you go. 10 real,
legitimate changes that happen in your
body from something as simple and cheap
as 5 g of creatine a day, and honestly,
most people never hear about half of
these because the conversation around
creatine gets stuck on the same tired
myths over and over again, year after
year. The truth is, this is genuinely
one of the most researched supplements
that exists on the market today with
decades of studies behind it, and the
data keeps holding up pretty
consistently across strength, recovery,
cognitive function, and even long-term
safety. Unlike a lot of trendy
supplements that pop up, get hyped for a
year, and then quietly disappear once
people realize they don't do much,
creatine has stuck around for a reason,
and that reason is simply that it keeps
proving itself study after study, decade
after decade. Now, I want to hear from
you. Are you currently taking creatine,
or is this video making you want to
finally start?
Drop a comment down below, and let me
know which one of these 10 changes
surprised you the most because I'm
genuinely curious which one hits
different depending on who's watching
and where you're at in your own fitness
journey. And hey, if this video actually
taught you something new today, do me a
favor and hit that like button,
subscribe if you're new around here so
you don't miss the next one, and I'll
catch you in the next video.

title: What Really Happens When You Take Creatine After 50 (Shocking Science)
text:
What Really Happens When You Take Creatine After 50 (Shocking Science)
Only 1% of people over 50 years old know the effects that creatine can have on the body. From the age of 50, our body begins to undergo significant changes. One of them, and perhaps the most concerning for many men, is the accelerated loss of muscle mass. This loss is not just an aesthetic issue. We're talking about a natural process called sarcopenia, which can reduce your physical strength by up to 15% per decade after 50 years of age. This means that simple daily tasks such as carrying groceries, climbing stairs, or even getting out of bed can become real challenges. But what if I told you that there is a supplement, accessible and well-studied, that can be a game-changer in this process? Yes, we're talking about creatine. In this video, you will see the five greatest benefits that adults experience when starting supplementation with creatine. The saddest thing is that despite all the scientifically proven benefits, less than 1% of people in this age group regularly consume this supplement. Why? Usually because of two common myths involving creatine.

title: You're Doing Lateral Raises Wrong! That's Why Your Shoulders Aren't Growing
text:
Track every set with Symmetry for free 👉🏼 https://symmetry.club/go/greengains

The outer edge of your shoulders is the side delt, and it's what makes you look wide from the front. Lateral raises should build it, but small habits hand the work to your legs, your traps or your front delts. Here are the seven most common mistakes, the fix for each, and a plan you can start this week.

• Momentum: if your knees, hips or lower back move, the dumbbell is too heavy. Torso still, only the arms travel
• Too high: stop when your elbows are level with your shoulders. Keep one fixed soft bend in your elbows, and stop a few inches before your thighs at the bottom
• No numbers: pick a dumbbell you can lift 12 to 20 clean times and end each set with 1 or 2 good reps left. Beat last week's numbers
• Shrugging: keep a gap between your shoulder and your ear at the top. Think wide, not up
• Counting on chest day: pressing trains the front of the shoulder; the side needs its own move
• Leftover sets: about 10 hard sets a week, split into 2 days of 5 sets, early in the session
• The twist: palms to the floor, thumbs forward at the top. A small tilt is fine; a big twist isn't

Rest at least 90 seconds between sets and keep it the same every week, so a bigger number means real progress. Cable or dumbbell: in an 8-week study, trained lifters grew their side delts about 4% thicker, and the arm trained with a cable grew about as much as the arm trained with a dumbbell. Give it 8 weeks before you judge it.

Some people do 300 push-ups a day,
every day for 6 full months, and when
the final video comes out after those 6
months, their chest and arms haven't
changed by a single centimeter. And
there's someone else who does 30
push-ups, but only three times a week.
And after two months, his chest is
bursting out of his shirt. His friends
ask him, "What did you do?" The
exercise is exactly the same: regular
push-ups on the floor. But the result
is completely different. What is the
difference between them? The difference
is not in the number of push-ups. The
push-up that either of them does. The
difference is in something
scientifically precise. Something no
one explains to you clearly. And today,
we’re going to reveal it number by
number. By the end of the video,
we’ll arrive at a specific number.
You can apply it exactly today, whether
you are at home or at the gym. Let’s
start with the first mistake that
almost every beginner makes. Your body
doesn’t know how to count numbers.
Meaning when you tell it, "I’m going
to do 100 push-ups today," it doesn’t
feel the number 100 at all; it feels
something called the proximity to
muscular failure. This concept was
studied in depth by a researcher named
Michael Zourdos at the University of
Tampa in America. He clarified in his
research that muscle doesn't grow
because you repeated a movement a large
number of times. Muscle grows because
you brought it close to a specific
point called muscular failure. Or
reached within one to three reps of it.
Meaning if you do 100 push-ups, but
every rep was easy and comfortable for
you, your body records it in its memory
. As a normal daily activity, just like
walking or climbing the stairs at home,
but if you do 30 push-ups and the last
ten become nearly impossible and your
arms are shaking, your body receives a
real emergency signal: "This challenge
is bigger than my current capacity, I
must build stronger muscle to handle it
next time." This specific signal is
what triggers the process of muscular
hypertrophy, not the number of
repetitions you brag about in front of
the camera. Okay, and this is the
question everyone wants the answer to.
Really, how many push-ups exactly? I
need a clear number, not general talk.
In a massive meta-analysis study,
published by Brad Schoenfeld. He is one
of the most famous researchers globally
in the field of muscle building and the
science of. Resistance training. He
combined dozens of studies in it. And
compared between few training sets and
many sets throughout the week. The
result was clear. The muscle needs
approximately between 10 to 20
effective sets per week for that single
muscle to get the maximum possible
growth, but the most important
discovery in the study, which most
people overlook, is that the first ten
sets give you the largest portion of
the total result, and the sets that
follow add very little improvement
compared to the effort exerted. Meaning
if you cannot commit to a huge training
volume every week, even four to six
effective sets per week are very
sufficient to build real, tangible
muscle, provided you reach close to
failure in every set. Here we arrive at
a point much more important than the
number itself. The type of push-up you
do changes everything. There is a vast
difference between a regular push-up, a
push-up with your feet elevated on a
chair, and a diamond push-up that
focuses on the triceps. And a slow
push-up with a four-second tempo on the
way down only. Each one of these types
changes the angle of pressure on the
muscle fibers and changes which muscle
takes the biggest load. A Japanese
researcher named Kei Kanehisa. He
studied the concept of Time Under
Tension in great detail. He found that
simply slowing the lowering phase to
four seconds instead of one.
Significantly increases muscle
activation. Even with the exact same
number of repetitions and the same
weight. Meaning you could do. Twenty
push-ups, but at a slow tempo. And with
full focus on the muscle. And get a
much better result than 50 fast, showy
push-ups in front of a camera with no.
Real benefit. Here is a question many
followers ask me: "Well, I work out at
home without weights, does this apply
to me?" The answer is yes, exactly.
Because your body doesn't distinguish
between gym iron weights and your own
body weight while doing push-ups. The
important thing is to reach the same
level of proximity to failure and to
increase the difficulty gradually.
Meaning if you are at home and regular
push-ups become easy, you can move to
decline push-ups, slow down the tempo,
or put a bag full of books on your back
. And if you are at the gym, you can
place an iron plate directly on your
back, or use a cable press machine. The
tool differs, but the scientific
principle remains the same, whether
you're in a gym equipped with the
latest machines or in your room with no
equipment. So, what is the biggest
mistake most people make without
exception? The mistake is stopping the
exercise as soon as they feel a little
fatigue, before they actually reach the
point of near failure. Your body
naturally loves comfort. And the first
signal of fatigue the brain sends tells
you, "That's enough, rest." But that is
precisely the moment when the exercise
actually starts working the muscle. The
last three to five repetitions where
you feel a distinct tremor and burning
in the muscle are the most valuable
reps in the entire set, and they are
what most people avoid without
realizing it. There is another very
dangerous point, which is repeating the
same thing without any increase over
time. If you do the same number of
push-ups every week in the exact same
way, your body will adapt completely
and stop growing. This is a
scientifically known phenomenon called
Progressive Overload. And if you don't
achieve it consistently, your body will
reach a plateau. Meaning you exert
yourself every day without any real
muscle progress, and you feel like all
your effort is going to waste. You must
increase the challenge every two weeks
or so, either by increasing the number
of reps, switching to a harder type of
push-up, slowing the tempo, or adding
extra weight to your back. So, after
all this scientific talk, the direct
practical answer you were waiting for:
If you want to build your chest,
shoulder, and tricep muscles using only
push-ups without any other equipment,
you need three to four sets per week
for each muscle. Each set should bring
you very close to failure. Meaning the
last two or three reps, you feel like
you can barely complete them and your
arms are shaking. Not 100 random
push-ups without focus, and not 30 just
to finish quickly and film a video. The
exact number changes from person to
person depending on their current
strength and training level. But the
feeling of proximity to failure is the
constant metric that works for everyone
without exception, whether a beginner
or someone who has been training for
years. And there is one final thing
more important than every number we
mentioned in this entire video:
nutrition and rest. If you train
perfectly and precisely, but don't eat
enough protein and don't sleep seven to
nine hours every night, your body won't
have the essential building blocks for
new muscle. Exercise only functions to
send a signal to your body that change
is required. But the body actually
builds during sleep, specifically in
the deep sleep stage where growth
hormone rises naturally and powerfully.
And here I must highlight a third
mistake, which is the hand placement
error. Many place their hands too far
apart, thinking it engages the chest
more. The result is that the shoulder
takes the brunt of the load instead of
the chest, and over time, they get
shoulder joint pain without knowing why
. The scientifically optimal position
is to have your hands at about
shoulder-width apart, angled slightly
outward. This balances the load between
the chest and triceps and significantly
reduces excess pressure on the joint.
Let me give you a simple weekly example
you can apply today, whether at home or
the gym: Monday: two to three sets of
regular push-ups to near failure.
Wednesday: two sets of push-ups at a
slow tempo (four seconds to descend).
Friday: a set of decline push-ups if
you're ready for a bigger challenge, or
regular push-ups with added resistance
if you are advanced. This simple
schedule alone, if you commit to it
with discipline for eight consecutive
weeks, will give you a clear difference
that you'll notice before anyone else
around you.

, meaning you make the muscle work in a

hypertrophy. And he published it in the

. And of course, don't forget what we

sleep quality and directly boosts
testosterone.

sitting, your testosterone is slowly
burning away. Sitting. Too long raises
cortisol, the stress hormone.

testosterone. Both cannot be high at the

testosterone goes down. Period. The
solutions: 1, the rule of. 50 minutes.

walk for 5 to 10 minutes. This alone
reduces cortisol and improves blood
circulation to the glands that produce
testosterone. Set an alarm on your phone
right now. 2: Interval training is the
most powerful for raising testosterone.

testosterone more than an hour of cardio
. The method: 30.
Seconds at your maximum energy, then 30
