subtitles.plaintext:
You can do push-ups every day and still
never break past 20 reps. Sounds
familiar, right? You train hard, you
stay consistent, but your numbers stay
stuck. So, what's the problem? Simple.
You've been training the wrong way. And
today, I'll show you the method that can
take you from 10 to over 80 push-ups in
one single set. It's brutal. It's
simple, and it works. But first, let's
get something straight.
Most people train push-ups like a
checklist. They do five sets of 15,
rest, repeat, and call it a day. But
that's not how real progress is made. If
you want serious results, you need to
train past your limits into that zone
where your body screams stop and your
mind says one more. That's where
strength is built. Now, before I reveal
the method, understand this. 99% of
people who try this quit in the first 4
days. because it burns, because it
humbles you. But the ones who push
through, they unlock levels of endurance
and strength they never thought
possible. So, if you're still here,
you're probably part of that 1%. Let's
begin. Number one, the secret method,
ladder push-ups. This is how it works.
You're going to stack push-up variations
in one continuous sequence from hardest
to easiest, each one to absolute
failure. Start with decline push-ups.
Your feet elevated, chest leading the
way. Go until your arms shake and you
can't do another clean rep. That's your
first ladder step. Immediately drop into
standard push-ups. No rest, no pause.
Same rule, push until failure. Next,
move into incline push-ups. Hands
elevated on a bench or chair. This
reduces the load just enough to let you
squeeze out more reps. Finally, finish
with knee push-ups. This is your last
stand. Empty the tank. Don't stop until
your arms literally give out. That's one
full ladder. Rest for a few minutes,
then repeat two or three more times. Do
this two to three sessions per week.
Trust me, your chest, shoulders, and
triceps will adapt fast. Number two, why
this works. Here's the science behind
the pain. By moving from harder
variations to easier ones, you're
extending time under tension. That's the
key to endurance and hypertrophy. Most
people fail because they stop the moment
their muscles fatigue. The ladder method
forces your body to keep working even as
it's exhausted, recruiting new muscle
fibers, improving stamina, and building
explosive strength. You're not just
doing more reps, you're training your
body to fight through fatigue. And
that's where real growth happens.
Number three, the rules that make or
break this. Rule number one, full range
of motion. Chest down, arms fully
extended at the top. Half reps equal
half results. Rule number two, no ego.
Don't chase numbers. Chase control.
Perfect form. Beats sloppy volume every
single time. Rule number three, recovery
matters. Your body doesn't grow during
the push-up, it grows between them.
Number four, when to add progression.
Once you can perform a full ladder
without collapsing, increase the
challenge. You can add tempo, go slower
on the way down, add volume, one extra
round each week, or upgrade your first
step to something harder, like archer or
pseudo plunchch push-ups. The goal is
simple. Never let your body get
comfortable. Number five, the mental
side. Here's the truth nobody tells you.
The difference between someone who can
do 20 push-ups and someone who can do
100 isn't strength, it's mindset. At 20
reps, your body gives up. At 40, your
mind gives up. At 80, both are
screaming. But the person who keeps
pushing anyway, that's the person who
transforms. Every rep past the limit
rewires your brain to stop quitting
early. That's how you build not just
muscle, but discipline. So, here's your
challenge. Try the ladder push-up method
for 2 months. Commit. Track your reps.
And when you finally crush 80 or more in
one set, remember this moment. You
didn't just build strength. You built
control, endurance, and a mindset that
refuses to quit. Now, it's your turn.
Comment below with how many push-ups you
can do right now, and come back after 4
weeks to see how far you've come. And if
you want full progressions to master
push-ups, plunchches, and handstands,
you know where to find me. This is
Phantom Core. See you in the next video.

What if I told you that you could build
a bigger, fuller, more dominant chest
using nothing more than two dumbbells?
Sounds hard to believe because most
people think bigger muscles only come
from lifting heavier and heavier
weights. But that's not actually how
muscle growth works. The truth is, if
you know how to use dumbbells correctly,
you can force your chest muscles to work
harder than many people do with heavy
barbells and expensive gym machines.
That's because muscles don't know how
much weight you're lifting. They only
know one thing, tension.
And today, I'm going to show you five
dumbbell chest exercises that create
incredible tension across your upper
chest, middle chest, lower chest, and
even the deep stabilizing muscles that
most people never train. These aren't
random exercises pulled from the
internet. Each one has a specific
purpose. One builds thickness, another
creates a deeper stretch. One targets
the stubborn upper chest, another
develops explosive pressing power. And
when you combine all five, your chest
starts looking wider, thicker, more
balanced, and noticeably stronger. Don't
make the mistake of skipping to the last
exercise. [music] Every movement in
today's workouts prepares your chest for
the next one. And by the time you reach
number one, your entire upper body will
be working together like never before.
So grab your dumbbells and let's start
building a chest that actually stands
out when you look in the mirror. Number
five, dumbbell guillotine press.
Let's begin with an exercise that almost
disappeared from modern gyms, yet
old-school bodybuilders absolutely loved
it. The dumbbell guillotine press.
At first glance, it looks similar to a
normal dumbbell press. But one small
difference completely changes how your
chest works. Instead of pressing with
your elbows tucked close to your body,
your elbows stay much wider. This
changes the line of force, placing far
more tension across the upper chest
fibers that many people struggle to
develop.
That's exactly why so many lifters
[music] have a flat looking chest from
the front. Their middle chest grows,
their shoulders get stronger, but the
upper chest never fills out. Without
that upper shelf, your chest never looks
complete. To perform this exercise
correctly, [music] lie flat on the bench
with your feet firmly planted. Hold a
dumbbell in each hand directly above
your chest. Keep your elbows flared
wider than a traditional [music] press.
Now, slowly lower the dumbbells toward
your upper chest, just below your
collarbone. Don't rush the movement.
Control every inch.
As you reach the bottom,
pause briefly.
Feel your upper chest stretching.
Then, drive the dumbbells back up while
squeezing your chest as hard as
possible.
Imagine trying to bring both sides of
your chest together.
That squeeze is where the magic happens.
One mistake many people make is turning
this into a shoulder press. If your
elbows move too far forward, your
shoulders take over and your chest loses
tension. Another mistake is bouncing
[music] the weight at the bottom.
Remember, muscles grow from controlled
tension, not from throwing weights
around. For muscle growth,
>> [music]
>> perform three to four sets of eight to
12 controlled repetitions.
Choose a weight that allows perfect form
from the first rep to the last. [music]
Master this movement and your upper
chest will finally start looking fuller.
But, having a strong upper chest alone
isn't enough.
If the middle portion of your chest
never experiences a deep stretch, your
overall chest can still look flat.
That's exactly why the next exercise
[music]
is so important. Number four, dumbbell
floor fly with pause. Most people think
a fly is simply about opening the arms,
then bringing them back together, but
that's why most people never feel their
chest working. The floor fly with pause
changes that completely. Instead of
using momentum, you'll force your chest
muscles to stay under tension [music]
during the most important part of the
movement. That short pause makes a huge
difference.
When your muscles remain stretched under
control, they recruit more muscle
fibers, creating the kind of stimulus
that's difficult to achieve with fast
repetitions.
Lie on the floor holding a dumbbell in
each hand. Your knees should stay bent,
feet flat on the ground. Press the
dumbbells above your chest, keeping a
slight bend in your elbows.
Now slowly lower both arms outward,
forming a wide arc. Lower until your
upper arms gently touch the floor. Don't
crash into it. The floor acts as a
safety stop, protecting your shoulders
while still allowing an excellent
stretch. Once your arms touch the floor,
pause for 1 full second. Don't relax.
Keep your chest tight.
Then squeeze your chest hard, bringing
both dumbbells back together in the same
arc. Imagine you're hugging a giant
[music] tree. That mental cue helps
activate the chest much more than simply
lifting the weights.
Many lifters move too quickly. Others
completely lock their elbows, placing
unnecessary stress on the joints. Keep
that slight bend throughout every
repetition.
Stay smooth. Stay controlled.
For best results, perform three sets of
10 to 15 repetitions, focusing on
quality rather than speed.
After finishing this movement, your
chest will feel fuller, warmer, and
ready for an exercise that specifically
attacks one of the hardest areas to
build, the upper inner chest, and that's
exactly where we're going next. Number
three, standing low-to-high dumbbell
fly. Now your middle chest is fully
activated, but there's still one area
that separates an average chest from an
impressive one. The upper inner chest.
This is the section that gives your
chest that lifted armor-like appearance.
And one of the best ways to target it
with dumbbells is the standing low to
high dumbbell fly. Unlike a traditional
fly, this movement [music] follows the
natural direction of your upper chest
fibers.
That means every repetition places
tension exactly where many people
struggle to build muscle. Stand with
your feet shoulder width apart. Hold a
dumbbell in each hand beside your
thighs. Keep a slight bend in your
elbows throughout the movement. Now,
instead of lifting the weight straight
forward, raise them in a wide arc,
moving from your hips upward and
slightly inward until both dumbbells
meet just in front of your upper chest.
At the very top, pause for a full second
and squeeze your chest as hard as you
possibly can.
Imagine trying to crush something
between your chest muscles.
That squeeze is what transforms this
exercise from [music] good into
exceptional.
Then slowly lower the dumbbells back
down, taking twice as long on the way
down as you did lifting them.
Remember, muscles don't grow while
lifting the weight. They grow while
controlling it.
One of the biggest mistakes people make
is turning this into a front raise. If
your arms stay too straight or you lift
with your shoulders, the upper chest
barely works. [music]
Instead, focus on pulling your arms
inward, not upward.
Another common mistake is rushing
through the movement. Every slow
repetition builds more tension, and more
tension usually means better muscle
stimulation. Perform three sets of 12 to
15 controlled repetitions. Don't chase
heavy weights here. Chase perfect
contractions. By now, your upper and
middle chest have been challenged from
different angles, but one important area
still hasn't received enough attention,
the lower chest, along with the muscles
that stabilize your rib cage and improve
pressing strength. That's exactly what
the next exercise is designed to fix.
Number two, dumbbell pullover press.
Most people think pullovers are only for
the lats. That's because they're doing
them wrong. When combined with a
controlled press, this movement becomes
one of the most underrated chest
builders you'll ever perform. [music]
The dumbbell pullover press doesn't just
train the lower chest. It also
strengthens your serratus anterior, the
muscle that gives your chest a more
[music] complete athletic appearance and
improves pressing stability.
Lie flat on a bench.
Hold one dumbbell with both hands above
your chest.
Keep your elbows slightly bent.
Now slowly lower the dumbbell behind
your head, feeling your chest and rib
[music] cage stretch. Don't force the
range of motion. Go only as far as you
can while staying comfortable and in
control.
Once you reach the bottom, pull the
dumbbell back over your chest, then
immediately perform a short chest press,
finishing directly above your chest
before beginning the next repetition.
This combination creates two powerful
forms of tension. First, the deep
stretch. Then, the powerful contraction.
Together, they force your chest to work
through a much larger range of motion
than a standard press.
A common mistake is bending the elbows
too much.
Another is letting the lower back arch
excessively.
Keep your core tight. Move slowly and
let your chest control every inch of the
movement. Perform three sets of eight to
12 repetitions. By this point, your
chest has experienced stretch, squeeze,
stability,
>> [music]
>> and controlled tension.
Now, it's time to finish with the
movement that brings everything
together. The exercise [music]
that combines strength, power,
coordination, and explosive upper body
development. Number one, dumbbell
deadlift to press.
This isn't just another chest exercise.
[music]
It's a movement that teaches your entire
body to generate force. Then, transfer
that force through your chest and
shoulders with every repetition. The
dumbbell deadlift to press is the
perfect finisher because it recruits
multiple muscle groups while demanding
explosive control. Place two dumbbells
on the floor. Stand with your feet about
shoulder width apart. Hinge at the hips.
Keep your chest up and grip the
dumbbells.
Drive through your legs. Stand up
powerfully. Then, immediately clean the
dumbbells to shoulder [music] level.
Without pausing, press them overhead in
one smooth motion.
Lower the dumbbells [music] back to your
shoulders, then back to the floor
under complete control. Repeat. This
exercise doesn't replace your chest
presses. It enhances them. The explosive
drive from your legs, combined with the
powerful press, forces your chest, front
delts, triceps, and core to work
together as one unit. Many people rush
this movement. Don't. Power comes from
control, not chaos. Keep your spine
neutral. Brace your core. Press with
intention. Every repetition should feel
smooth, strong, and explosive. Perform
three to four sets of six to 10
repetitions. Focus on quality, not
speed. When done correctly, this
movement finishes your workout by
challenging muscles that are already
fatigued, helping you build strength
that carries over into every other
pressing exercise. [music]
Let's quickly recap today's workout.
Number five, dumbbell guillotine press
for building a fuller upper chest.
Number four,
dumbbell floor fly with pause to create
a deep stretch and thicker middle chest.
Number three, standing low to high
dumbbell
fly to bring out the upper inner chest.
Number two, dumbbell pullover press to
develop the lower chest and strengthen
the serratus.
Number one, dumbbell deadlift to press
to build explosive upper body power and
tie everything together.
You don't need a room full of expensive
machines and you don't need to lift the
heaviest weights in the gym.
Sometimes, all it takes is two
dumbbells, the right exercises, and
consistent effort. Stay patient, focus
on perfect form, and your chest won't
just get stronger. It will start looking
noticeably bigger, fuller, and more
balanced every time you look in the
mirror. Now, I want to hear from you.
Which one of these five exercises are
you going to try first?
Comment the exercise number below. I
read every comment and I'd love to know
which movement you're adding to your
next chest workout.
And if you enjoy practical
science-backed workouts that actually
help you build real muscle, make sure to
subscribe to Phantom Core and turn on
notifications because the next workout
might be exactly what your body has been
missing.

subtitles.plaintext:
You train hard, push-ups, pull-ups,
squats, always chasing the next rep. But
what if I told you the most powerful way
to build strength is to not move at all?
That's right. You can reshape your
entire body, your strength, posture, and
control by holding still. Today, I'll
show you four isometric holds that will
completely transform your physique. No
weights, no motion, no excuses. Let's
begin. Number one,
the wall sit.
It looks harmless, just you against a
wall.
But 30 seconds in, your legs start to
shake, your quads catch fire, and your
mind wants out. That's when the
transformation starts.
Slide down the wall until your thighs
are parallel to the floor, knees at 90°,
and your back flat.
No arching, no leaning forward, just
tension.
This static hold forces every muscle in
your legs to contract at once. Quads,
glutes, and hamstrings.
It builds strength like squats, but with
zero impact. Hold for 20 seconds to
start, then push toward one full minute.
Stay still, breathe slow, and let the
burn sculpt your legs.
Because this is more than a leg
exercise, it's mental warfare.
Number two, the plank. Everyone thinks
they know it, but most people do it
wrong. The plank isn't just a core move,
it's a full body test of control. From
your shoulders to your toes, every
muscle fights to hold that perfect line.
Elbows under shoulders, body straight,
core tight, glutes squeezed. No sagging
hips, no lifted backs, just pure
stability. Start with 30 seconds.
When it feels easy, try 60. And if you
really want to challenge yourself, go
side plank or lift one arm, one leg. Do
it right, and your entire frame
tightens. Your core gets solid, your
posture improves, and your balance
skyrockets. Because strength isn't how
much you lift, it's how well you hold.
Number three, the Superman hold. You
can't see your back in the mirror, but
everyone sees it when you stand tall.
This is how you build that posture. Lie
flat, arms stretched forward, and lift
your arms, chest, and legs off the
ground. Hold 20 seconds, maybe 30. Feel
your glutes and spinal muscles locking
in, keeping your spine straight and
strong. This hold counters hours of
sitting, fixes slouching, and builds the
foundation for every pull-up, every
lift. It's simple, but brutal. Hold your
ground, breathe, and rise again. Because
the real strength is built in the
muscles you forget to train.
Number four, the isometric push-up.
Hold. Now it's time for the upper body.
Drop into a push-up position, lower
halfway, then stop. Freeze. Every fiber
in your chest, arms, and shoulders
screams to move, but don't. Hold. This
position forces your muscles to contract
under constant tension. It builds
explosive power and endurance at once.
Start with 15 seconds, work toward 30.
Three to four sets.
Rest between each one, and never rush
it. This is precision strength.
Because what looks easy, holding still,
is actually the hardest test of control.
Here's how to bring it all together.
Each exercise is a full body lock. Wall
sit, three sets of 30 to 60 seconds.
Plank, three sets of 30 to 60 seconds.
Superman hold, three sets of 20 to 30
seconds.
Push-up hold, three sets of 15 to 30
seconds.
Do this routine three times a week.
Every session will feel short, but
intense.
In just a few weeks, your posture,
stability, and strength will look and
feel completely different.
Isometric training teaches something
deeper than movement. It teaches
control, the ability to resist, endure,
and focus.
Because strength isn't always about
motion, sometimes it's about stillness.
Holding when your body wants to quit,
enduring the burn when everything tells
you to drop. That's how you build real
strength, the kind that lasts.

subtitles.plaintext:
He trains 6 days a week, 15 exercises
per session, 2 hours each time, and
posts "No Days Off" on his story. He
does three 30-minute sessions per week.
He rests between sets, he sleeps, and
in a year, guess which one will have
gained the most muscle. The second one,
not because he's more motivated, but
because he's a "Lazybones." But a smart
Lazybones; he knows exactly what makes
a muscle grow and ignores everything
else. So, here is the Lazybones method
for gaining muscle. Bodyweight, no gym,
with the least effort possible. Five
rules, and the third one, almost no one
applies. Rule number 1: 2 to 3 sessions
per week, no more. Your muscle doesn't
grow during your session. During the
session, you damage it. It's afterwards
, during rest days, that your body
repairs and rebuilds it a bit stronger.
If you keep hammering the same muscle
every day, you never give it time to
finish the construction work. Studies
comparing training frequencies are
quite clear. Working a muscle twice a
week works better than once, and beyond
that, it adds almost nothing more. So
the Lazybones does three full-body
sessions: Monday, Wednesday, Friday.
The other days, he walks, he lives his
life, and he feels no guilt. Rule
number 2, few exercises but the right
ones. The "No Days Off" guy does
push-ups, wide push-ups, narrow
push-ups, decline push-ups, flys, dips,
and three more variations seen on
TikTok. The Lazybones covers his whole
body with four movements. One for
pushing: push-ups or dips. One for
pulling: pull-ups or rows under a table
if you don't have a bar. One for the
legs: squats, and one for the core.
With those four, everything else is
just decoration. Rule number 3, the one
that almost no one applies. Each set
must end near failure. That's where
everything is decided. What makes a
muscle grow isn't the easy first reps,
it's the last ones. The ones where you
slow down, where it burns, where you're
no longer sure you can do one more. The
Lazybones doesn't do many sets, but he
takes each one to within one to three
reps of failure. And that is very good
news for you if you train at home.
Researchers compared heavy sets of
around 10 reps and light sets of 30
reps or more. When both go to failure,
the muscle grows about the same. In
other words, you don't need a huge load
. Your body weight is enough on one
condition: reach the end of the set.
The guy who does 50 easy push-ups while
looking at his phone is doing volume,
not building muscle. Rule number 4:
make the exercise a little harder. Over
time, your body adapts to what you ask
of it. If you do the exact same workout
for 6 months, it has no reason to
change. So, the slacker tracks their
workouts and when they can do their
sets cleanly, they add a rep or two and
when it gets too easy, they move to a
harder variation. Classic push-ups
become elevated-foot push-ups. Squats
become jump squats and then single-leg
squats. For pull-ups, they perform the
descent more slowly. No need to change
everything, just a small step up. From
time to time. Rule number 5: rest is
part of training. Between two sets, the
slacker sits for 1 to 2 minutes to
catch their breath. And they're right;
if they go straight through without a
break, the next set is botched. And a
botched set doesn't do much. And at
night, they sleep 7 to 9 hours. Just
one week of too little sleep is enough
to lower muscle production. Add to that
enough protein, around 1g per kilo of
body weight daily, and you've done the
essential. Now, here is everything the
slacker ignores without any guilt:
muscle soreness. Being sore the next
day doesn't mean the workout was good.
It just means your body wasn't used to
it. The famous 30-minute window to
drink your protein after the session.
What counts is what you eat throughout
the day, not the exact minute.
Complicated programs, arm day, shoulder
day, and the idea that you have to
surprise your muscle with a new
exercise every week. No, the muscle
isn't surprised, it's just tired. What
does that look like in practice? Monday
, Wednesday, Friday: push-ups, pull-ups
, squats, planks. Three sets of each,
stopping one or two reps short of
failure. 2 minutes of rest between sets
, 35 minutes and it's done. Every week,
you try to do a little better than the
week before. And meanwhile, the "no
days off" guy is on his 3rd week
without a rest day. His shoulders are
killing him, his workouts are getting
weaker and weaker, and he's starting to
wonder why he’s stopped making
progress. The lazy guy, on the other
hand, is fresh and making progress. And
if even thinking about your workouts is
too much effort for you, I’ve got
just the thing. My app generates
workouts adapted to your level and
goals that you can do anywhere. The
link is in the description. The lazy
guy doesn't put in less effort than the
others, he just does what matters. Yeah
.

Take a look at your arms for a second.
>> [music]
>> Have you ever noticed something strange?
Some people have decent biceps. They
train hard every week. They can curl
heavy dumbbells. Yet, somehow, their
arms still don't look impressive.
Now, compare that to someone with truly
well-developed arms. Even in a simple
t-shirt, their arms immediately stand
out. They look stronger, more athletic,
and far more complete. So, what's the
difference? It isn't always genetics. It
isn't always heavier weights. And it
definitely isn't doing hundreds of curls
every week. The real difference is
understanding that your arms are built
by more than just your biceps. In fact,
human anatomy tells us something most
people completely overlook. Your triceps
make up nearly 2/3 of your upper arms
muscle mass.
Your forearms influence not only how
your arms look, but also how well you
grip, pull, carry, and even perform many
upper body exercises. And your biceps,
they're only one piece of the puzzle.
That's why so many people spend months
chasing bigger arms, while unknowingly
leaving huge amounts of muscle
completely under-trained.
Research in strength training continues
to show that muscle development depends
on much more than simply lifting heavier
weights. Exercise selection, range of
motion, controlled tempo, and mechanical
tension all influence how your muscles
are challenged. That's exactly why
today's workout is different. I'm going
to show you six carefully selected
dumbbell exercises designed to train
your arms from multiple angles.
Some emphasize the long head of the
biceps. Some target the often neglected
brachialis.
Others place your triceps under greater
stretch, or strengthen the forearms that
support nearly every lift you perform.
Every exercise [music]
has a purpose. Every movement fills is
gap that traditional arm workouts often
miss.
By the end of this workout, you won't
just know six new exercises. You'll
understand why each one deserves a place
in your training. So, grab a pair of
dumbbells, slow down, [music] focus on
quality over ego, and let's begin with
an exercise that many experienced
lifters quietly rely on, but
surprisingly few people perform
correctly.
Number six, dumbbell drag curl.
Let's start with a simple question.
Why do so many people perform endless
bicep curls, yet never develop that high
rounded bicep peak they're chasing? The
answer often comes down to one thing,
elbow position. During a traditional
dumbbell curl, your elbows usually stay
beside your torso. [music]
It works well, but it isn't the only way
to challenge the biceps.
The dumbbell drag curl changes the
mechanics of the movement. Instead of
allowing the dumbbells to travel
forward, you keep them close to your
body, while your elbows move slightly
behind you as the weight rises.
This subtle change shifts the emphasis
toward the long head of the biceps,
the portion that contributes [music] to
the appearance of a taller bicep peak.
Biomechanics research suggests that
changing shoulder and elbow position can
influence how different regions of the
elbow flexors contribute during a curl.
That's one reason why exercise variation
matters, not because one exercise is
magic, but because different movement
patterns challenge muscles in different
ways.
To perform the drag curl correctly,
stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand.
Keep your chest lifted, shoulders
relaxed, and core
>> [music]
>> tight. Now begin curling the dumbbells
upward, but instead of letting them
swing away from your body, drag them
upward along your torso. Your elbows
should naturally travel backward, while
the dumbbells stay close to your body
from [music] start to finish. There's no
swinging, no leaning back, no momentum.
At the very top,
pause for a brief second, squeeze your
biceps as hard as you can, then lower
the weight slowly over two to three
seconds.
That controlled lowering phase is just
as important as the lift itself.
>> [music]
>> Many lifters make the mistake of turning
this into a regular curl.
Others use weights that are too heavy,
forcing their shoulders to take [music]
over.
Remember, if your body is moving more
than your arms, you're probably lifting
too much.
Choose a weight that allows complete
control. Quality contractions always
outperform sloppy repetitions. Perform
three to four sets of eight to 12
repetitions,
focusing on smooth movement, full range
of motion, and a powerful squeeze at the
top.
Once your long head begins receiving
consistent tension, your biceps can
start looking noticeably fuller.
But your arms still aren't complete
because underneath the biceps lies
another muscle, one that many people
never think about.
>> [music]
>> Yet it has the power to make your entire
arm appear thicker, and that's exactly
where we're going next. [music] Number
five, Zottman curl.
At first glance, the Zottman curl looks
like an ordinary dumbbell curl, but
don't let its simplicity fool you. This
single movement combines two different
grips, allowing you to challenge
multiple muscles during the same
repetition.
Research into forearm and elbow flexor
function has shown that changing [music]
hand position can alter which muscles
contribute more throughout the movement.
That's exactly what makes this exercise
so valuable. Begin by standing with a
dumbbell in each hand.
Start with your palms facing forward.
Curl both dumbbells towards your
shoulders under complete control. Once
you reach the top, rotate [music] your
wrists so your palms now face downward.
Then slowly lower the dumbbells in that
overhand position. [music]
At the bottom, rotate your hands back to
the starting position and repeat. That
simple rotation changes everything. On
the way up, your biceps perform most of
the work. On the way down, your
brachialis and forearm muscles are
forced [music] to control the weight,
creating a completely different training
stimulus than a standard curl. One of
the biggest mistakes people make is
rushing through the wrist rotation.
Don't. Every part of this movement
should feel smooth, controlled, and
deliberate. Another common mistake is
dropping the weights too quickly during
the lowering phase. Remember, the
eccentric portion of a lift plays an
important [music]
role in resistance training. Control it.
Don't fight against it.
For best results, perform three sets of
10 to 12 repetitions using moderate
weights.
By the end of this exercise, your biceps
will already feel different. Your
forearms will begin working harder and
your grip will be challenged in a way
that ordinary curls simply can't
replicate.
But despite all that work, we still
haven't trained the largest muscle of
your upper arm, the muscle that
contributes the most to overall arm
size. And that's exactly where we're
headed next. Number four, cross body
dumbbell triceps extension. By now, your
biceps, brachialis, and forearms have
already been challenged. But if your
goal is to build bigger looking arms,
there's one muscle you simply cannot
ignore, the long head of the triceps.
Remember what we mentioned at the
beginning? Your triceps make up nearly
2/3 of your upper arm. So, if they're
under developed, your arms will never
reach their full potential, no matter
how many curls you perform.
Here's something many lifters don't
realize. The long head of the triceps
crosses the shoulder joint.
Because of that, changing the position
of your arm changes how much tension
this muscle experiences. That's one
reason why overhead and cross-body
extensions have become popular in many
strength training programs. The
cross-body dumbbell triceps extension
takes advantage of that principle.
[music]
Lie flat on a bench, hold one dumbbell
in each hand directly above your
shoulders. Now, bend one arm bringing
the dumbbell diagonally across your body
toward the opposite shoulder. Pause
briefly. Then, extend your arm back to
the starting position using your triceps
[music]
to control the movement. Don't let
gravity take over. Move slowly. Stay
smooth. Focus on feeling the back of
your upper arm doing the work. One
common mistake is allowing the elbow to
drift outward. Keep it stable.
Another mistake is lowering the dumbbell
too quickly. Control the descent. The
lowering phase creates valuable training
stimulus when performed correctly.
Choose a weight you can manage with
perfect form. Perform three sets of 10
to 12 repetitions per arm.
Once your triceps begin catching up with
your biceps, your entire arm starts
looking thicker even before you gain
significant body weight. But, we're not
finished yet because there's another
exercise that keeps almost constant
tension on the triceps
while reducing unnecessary shoulder
involvement. And that's exactly what
comes next. Number three, dumbbell Tate
press. At first glance, the Tate press
looks unusual. And that's probably why
so few people include it in their
workouts.
But, don't let the movement fool you.
This exercise was designed to place the
emphasis where many pressing exercises
don't. Your triceps. Unlike a standard
dumbbell press, the elbows stay flared
outward while the dumbbells move toward
the center of your chest. This unique
[music] path reduces the contribution
from larger muscles, allowing the
triceps to take on more of the workload.
Research in resistance training
consistently shows that muscle
activation changes depending on joint
position and movement path.
That's exactly why exercise variety
matters.
Lie on a flat bench. Hold two dumbbells
[music]
directly above your chest. Turn the ends
of the dumbbells toward each other. Now
slowly bend your elbows,
bringing the inside ends of the
dumbbells toward the center of your
chest.
Pause briefly,
then press the weights back to the
starting [music] position.
Don't rush. Every repetition should feel
controlled. Avoid bouncing the weights.
Avoid locking out aggressively.
Let the triceps stay under tension
throughout the set.
Another mistake is choosing weights that
are far too heavy.
Remember, this isn't an ego lift. It's a
precision movement. Use a weight you can
fully control. Perform three sets of 10
to 15 repetitions. By now, your biceps
have been challenged. Your forearms have
worked. Your triceps are beginning to
fatigue. But there's still one muscle
hiding underneath your biceps.
A muscle that many people never
intentionally train, even though it can
make your arms look noticeably thicker.
Let's fix that. Number two.
Hammer curl with pause. Most people
think bigger arms come from bigger
biceps, but that's only part of the
story. Underneath the biceps sits the
brachialis.
As this muscle develops, it can help
push the biceps upward,
>> [music]
>> creating the appearance of fuller arms,
the hammer curl with pause targets this
area while also strengthening the
brachioradialis in your forearms.
Stand tall holding a dumbbell in each
hand with a neutral grip, palms facing
each other.
Curl both dumbbells upward
>> [music]
>> keeping your elbows close to your sides.
Once the dumbbells reach shoulder
height, pause for two full seconds.
Don't relax, keep squeezing.
Then slowly lower the weights under
complete control.
That pause isn't there to make the
exercise harder for no reason. It
encourages greater control, reduces
momentum,
>> [music]
>> and helps you focus on the muscles doing
the work. A common mistake is swinging
the body backward. Another is shortening
the range of motion. Lift through the
full movement, lower through the full
movement. Every repetition should look
almost identical.
Perform three to four sets of eight to
12 repetitions. At this point, every
major muscle of your arms has been
challenged.
But there's one final exercise.
One that delivers one of the strongest
contractions your biceps can experience,
and that's why it earns the number one
position.
Number one, dumbbell spider curl.
If your goal is to finish an arm workout
with complete control, maximum
contraction, and minimal cheating, few
exercises do it better than the spider
curl. Unlike standing curls, your upper
arms stay fixed against an incline
bench. That means momentum has nowhere
to hide. Your biceps must do nearly all
the work. Set an incline bench to
approximately 45°.
Lie chest down against the bench. Allow
your arms to hang naturally toward the
floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand. Now curl
the weights upward without moving your
elbows.
Focus on bringing your little finger
slightly higher at the top.
Pause. Squeeze your biceps as hard as
possible.
Then lower the dumbbells slowly, taking
at least 3 seconds to reach the bottom.
Don't allow the weights to simply fall.
[music] Control every inch. Many lifters
try to lift too heavy, but the spider
curl rewards precision, not momentum.
Use a moderate weight. Stay strict. Feel
every repetition. Perform three sets of
10 to 12 repetitions. When performed
consistently, this exercise can become
an excellent finishing movement because
it emphasizes quality contractions after
the rest of your arm muscles are already
fatigued. Let's quickly bring everything
together. Today's workout wasn't
designed to chase heavier dumbbells. It
was designed to train every major muscle
that gives your arms their size, shape,
and strength.

brachialis, and forearm development.

for placing greater emphasis on the long
head of the triceps.
Dumbbell Tate press for continuous
triceps focused tension. [music]
Hammer curl with pause for building
thicker looking arms through the
brachialis and brachioradialis.
Dumbbell spider curl for finishing with
maximum biceps control and contraction.
Remember, [music] building impressive
arms isn't about doing one perfect
exercise. It's about training your
biceps, triceps, and forearms together
using different movement patterns,
[music] good technique, and consistent
effort over time. Now, I'd love to hear
from you. Which one of these six

workouts that help you build muscle with
smarter training, subscribe to Phantom
Core because your next breakthrough
[music] might start with your very next
workout.

These movements attack belly fat from
[music] every angle. They force your

And the best part, your metabolism stays

Number two, jump rope. The exercise you

[music] Feet hip width. Bar over the

Humans are built for endurance, [music]

text:

translatedText:
100 push-ups a day for 30 days: on paper, it's the perfect challenge. No gym, no equipment. In reality, the first day hurts… and around the third week, something happens that no one tells you about.

👉 My app, which generates workouts adapted to your level, that you can do anywhere: https://linktr.ee/Kardyo

Day 1, Day 2, Day 7, Day 12, Day 18, Day 30: what really changes in your body, and how to make it work until the end.

subtitles.plaintext:
100 push-ups a day for 30 days. On
paper, it's the perfect challenge. No
gym, no equipment, 10 minutes a day. In
real life, on the first day, you're
going to regret it. And around the 3rd
week, something is going to happen that
nobody tells you about. The challenge
will stop working. We'll see why, what
really changes in your body after 30
days, and how to make it work until the
end. Day 1, you get into position, you
start counting, motivated. 10, 15, 20
if you've already got some experience.
And then, your arms shake, your chest
burns, and you've still got 80 left.
It's normal; if you're a beginner, you
won't do 100 push-ups in a row. Nobody
is asking you to. The idea is 100
push-ups throughout the day, not in one
single set. You break it down into 10
sets of 10 spread throughout the day,
or five sets of 20 if you're more
comfortable. One set in the morning,
one before eating, one when coming home
from work. At the end of the day, the
counter shows 100. But before you count
, every push-up must count. Because
doing push-ups poorly is just an
opportunity to hurt your shoulders.
Hands a little wider than your
shoulders. Body braced, straight as a
board, from your heels to your head.
Your butt shouldn't go up, your stomach
shouldn't sag. Elbows at about 45 °
from your body, not flared out
horizontally like a T. And you go down
until your chest grazes the floor, not
halfway down. A half-push-up is a
half-push-up. It doesn't count. If you
can't do 10 clean ones, no shame in
that. Drop your knees or put your hands
on a table, a bench, the edge of the
sofa. The higher your hands are, the
easier it is. You do your 100 like that
and lower your position little by
little. Day 2. You wake up, you reach
out to grab your phone, and your chest
reminds you what you did yesterday.
Soreness in your pecs, triceps, and the
front of your shoulders. It's not
lactic acid, contrary to what you hear
everywhere. It's micro-tears in the
muscle and the resulting inflammation
because your body isn't used to this
movement. It arrives the next day and
is often worse the day after that. The
good news is that it doesn't last. Your
body adapts very quickly to this kind
of effort. By the second or third
session, the soreness is much milder,
even while doing the same thing. So on
day two, you do your hundred, maybe
more slowly or in more sets if you have
to, but you do them. Day 7, the end of
the first week, and something
surprising happens. Your sets are
easier. Where you were stuck at 15, you
might now do 20 and tell yourself, "
This is it, I'm building muscle." Not
yet, bro. What has changed is primarily
your brain. In the first few weeks,
most of the strength you gain comes
from your nervous system. Your brain
learns the movement, activates more
fibers at once, coordinates them better
, and all the muscles working together
stop getting in each other's way. The
muscle is practically the same as it
was a week ago. It’s just better
controlled. That’s why beginners
progress so quickly at first, and
that’s why you shouldn't get carried
away. Day 12. The soreness has
disappeared. The challenge becomes a
routine, and that’s often when
another, more subtle pain arrives. A
wrist that pulls, or a shoulder that
pinches at the bottom of the movement.
Your muscle adapts in a few days, but
your tendons and joints adapt much more
slowly. And doing the same movement 100
times every day without a single rest
day. That is exactly the kind of load
that ends up irritating them. So, three
rules. One, check your elbows. If they
flare out horizontally, it’s often
your shoulder that pays the price. Two,
if it's your wrists, do your push-ups
on your fists or on handles to keep
your wrists straight. Three, pain in a
joint is not muscle soreness. Lower the
volume, let a few days pass, and if it
doesn't go away, go see someone. A 30-
day challenge isn't worth 3 months with
a busted shoulder. Day 18. And here is
the moment I was telling you about at
the beginning. The challenge is
becoming easy, too easy. You breeze
through your sets of 10 without
breaking a sweat. Maybe you're doing
your hundred in three sets. You feel
strong, and you're right. Except this
is when your body stops having a reason
to change. Your body only adapts to
what you demand of it, nothing more.
Muscle grows when it is pushed near its
limit. When the last repetitions of a
set become really hard, those are the
ones that send the signal. A set of 10
when you could do 30 is just a warm-up.
You can do 100, 200, 300 like that.
You'll mostly just become more enduring
. Your body has done the math. If
push-ups are easy, it knows how to do
them. It doesn't need to build any more
. That's the trap of all fixed-number
challenges. The number stays the same.
You, you change. And the challenge that
brought you to your knees on day 1 asks
nothing of you by day 18. The solution
isn't to move up to 200, it's to make
each push-up harder. You lower yourself
in 3 seconds instead of one. You pause
for a second at the bottom, chest just
off the floor. You elevate your feet on
a chair. The higher the feet, the more
weight you carry and the more your
shoulders and upper pecs work. You
bring your hands closer to load the
triceps. With that, your sets of 10
become real sets again. Maybe you're
only doing 60 push-ups a day now. That
doesn't matter. 60 hard push-ups do
more for your muscles than 100 easy
ones. Day 30. End of the challenge.
You've done nearly 3,000 push-ups. What
has really changed? First, your
strength. Your maximum in a row has
probably gone up significantly. That's
the clearest and quickest result. Next,
the muscle. Yes, it has started to grow
. The first measurable signs often
appear after 3 or 4 weeks. But
measurable by ultrasound, not
necessarily in the mirror. You might
see pecs that are a bit fuller, triceps
a bit firmer. No one on the street is
going to ask you what your secret is.
And your belly? Sorry, push-ups are
barely a few dozen calories. About half
a cookie. Your core has worked because
a push-up is also a moving plank. But
to see your abs, it happens mostly on
your plate, not on the mat. And then
there's the real result, the one you
don't see. For 30 days, you trained
every single day, even on the days you
didn't want to. That is rare. But be
careful, 30 days isn't enough for it to
become automatic. In a well-known study
on habits, it took an average of over 2
months for a new action to become
automatic. In other words, if you stop
on day 31, there's a good chance you
won't get back to it. So, what would I
do in your place? For the first two
weeks, I would do exactly the challenge
. 100 push-ups a day in sets with clean
technique. It's perfect for learning
the movement and building the habit.
Next, I'll stop counting to 100. I'll
switch to three or four sessions a week
with a few hard sets until the last two
or three reps are really difficult. And
each week, one push-up harder than the
week before, with rest days so your
joints can keep up. And above all, I
won't just be pushing. You also have to
pull with pull-ups or rowing under a
table for your back. And your legs,
they exist too. And if you don't want
the hassle of building all that, that's
exactly what my app does. It generates
sessions adapted to your level and your
goal that you can do anywhere. The link
is in the description. 100 push-ups a
day is a very good start. The problem
is believing it's a program.

subtitles.plaintext:
Two guys start on the same Monday. The
first does strength training: push-ups,
pull-ups, squats three times a week.
The second starts running three times a
week, as well. Same age, same starting
point, same motivation. A year later,
we put them side by side. Which one has
changed the most? The answer will
surprise you because they didn't change
in the same way. Their hearts aren't
the same shape, their muscles aren't
producing the same things. And if they
both stop tomorrow, one will lose a
huge chunk of his year in 3 months, the
other much less. So, we’re going to
follow them month after month. What
changes in their bodies and what
doesn't. And at the end, I'll introduce
you to a third guy, the one who beats
them both without doing a single extra
session. First week, the strength
training guy does his first push-ups.
He does eight, he shakes, and the next
day, he struggles to lift his arms. The
runner lasts 10 minutes before he's out
of breath. Two days later, his calves
hurt when he goes down the stairs. Both
are sore. These are small lesions in
the muscle that the body repairs and
strengthens. Good news, by the second
week, the same session hurts much less.
The muscle has learned to protect
itself. Week 3. And here, something
strange happens with the strength
training guy. He does 12 push-ups
instead of 8, 50%more. But when he
looks in the mirror, nothing has
changed, not 1 mm of extra arm. So,
where does this strength come from?
From his brain. In the first few weeks,
it's not the muscle growing, it's the
nervous system learning. It activates
more fibers at the same time and in the
right order. Researchers measured this
as early as the late 70s. At the start
of a program, the majority of strength
gains come from the nerves. The muscle
itself follows later. For the runner,
it's also the engine that changes first
, but not the same one. In a few weeks,
his body produces more plasma, the
liquid part of the blood. With more
volume in the pipes, his heart sends
more blood with every beat. Therefore,
it doesn't need to beat as fast. His
resting pulse starts to drop. The 10
minutes become 20, then 30. At 6 weeks,
both are stronger. But if you take
their picture, they look exactly the
same as on day one. This is the moment
when most people give up. Right at the
moment it was starting to work. Second
month, the gym guy finally starts to
see something. His shoulders take on a
bit of shape, his arms fill his t-shirt
a bit more. This is the start of
hypertrophy, the muscle actually
getting bigger. And it mainly happens
in one case, when those sets go close
to failure. The last repetitions, the
ones that burn, are the ones that give
the order to build. If he keeps doing
the same eight easy push-ups all year,
he won't gain almost anything.
Meanwhile, inside the runner's muscles,
something invisible is happening. These
cells are creating more mitochondria.
These are the little power plants that
turn fat and sugar into energy using
oxygen. The more he has, the longer he
can run without getting out of breath.
His legs don't get much bigger, they
just become much more enduring. Do you
see the difference yet? One is building
a bigger engine, the other is making
his engine more efficient, and it’s
even more visible in your body's most
important muscle. Third month, the
heart. It’s the most astonishing
change in the whole story. Your heart
is a muscle and it adapts to what you
ask of it, just like the others. The
runner asks his heart to pump a lot of
blood for a long time. So, over the
years, in endurance athletes, the heart
gets bigger on the inside. It can fill
up more and send out more blood with
every beat. That's why some runners
have a resting pulse below 50. The gym
guy, meanwhile, asks his heart to push
hard in bursts when he strains during a
set. In strength athletes, it's more
the heart wall that thickens a bit.
Researchers compared the two as early
as the 70s using ultrasound. Two
trained hearts, two different shapes.
Mind you, for someone training three
times a week, these changes remain
small, but the direction is correct.
Your heart becomes what you make it do.
And the scale in all this, that's where
both get it wrong. After 3 months, the
runner has lost 3 kg. He is happy. The
gym guy, for his part, has lost almost
nothing on the scale. He is
disappointed. He's wrong because he
lost fat too, but he gained a bit of
muscle at the same time. On the scale,
the two cancel each other out. On waist
measurement, no. He lost 2 cm off his
waist and his clothes fit better. The
scale doesn't see the difference
between 1 kg of fat and 1 kg of muscle.
Your mirror? Yes. And the story about
muscle burning calories even when you
sleep, it's true, but much less than
people say. 1 extra kg of muscle burns
about 13 calories a day at rest. Not
even a square of chocolate. The real
advantage of muscle isn't there. We'll
come back to that later. 6 months, we
put them side by side. The gym guy does
25 push-ups, his first pull-ups, and
you start to see the difference when he
takes his shirt off. The runner runs
for 45 minutes without stopping, goes
up stairs without thinking, and his
resting heart rate has dropped several
beats. Each has gained something the
other doesn't have. And this is where
it gets interesting, because in 3
months, both will hit the same wall,
and a little later, one of them will
discover that a good part of what he
built can melt away in a few weeks. 9
months. The wall. Both run into the
same problem. Progress is no longer as
fast. It's normal; the body adapts to
what is asked of it. If you always ask
it for the same thing, it has no reason
to change. The runner who always does
the same 30 minutes at the same pace
stagnates. The one who continues to
progress is the one who varies things.
A slightly longer run, a slightly
faster run. The gym guy who always does
his 25 push-ups also stagnates. The one
who keeps going is the one who makes
the exercise harder. Feet elevated, a
slower descent, a weighted backpack,
one more rep, or something a bit harder
each session. It's the same rule for
both. You don't progress by doing the
same thing for longer. You progress by
making it a little bit harder. Now for
bones, nobody thinks about them, yet
your bones are alive. They strengthen
when they receive impacts or loads and
they weaken when they don't. The runner
takes impacts with every stride. His
legs and hips benefit, but his upper
body receives almost nothing. The gym
guy, meanwhile, puts a load everywhere.
Arms, shoulders, back, legs. And
studies show that for a bone, the
intensity of the load matters more than
the number of repetitions. A few heavy
efforts are worth more than thousands
of small ones. 1 year. Let's put them
side by side one last time. The
weightlifter has gained a few kilos of
muscle, does pull-ups and tough
push-ups, lost his belly, and is strong
all over, but run up three flights of
stairs with him and he'll be out of
breath. The runner can run for an hour.
His heart beats slowly at rest. His
stamina has changed, he has lost weight
. But ask him to do 10 proper push-ups
or even one pull-up, and it's a
struggle. Neither one won. They simply
trained two different things. And now,
the question no one asks. What happens
if they stop? Imagine work, an injury,
or laziness; they stop everything for 3
months, and the runner loses it fast.
In studies, stamina begins to drop
after just 2 to 3 weeks. Blood volume
goes back down, and mitochondria
decrease. After a few months, a huge
part of his year is gone. The
weightlifter loses too, but much more
slowly. Strength often lasts several
weeks, and when he resumes, he recovers
faster than he progressed the first
time. Researchers think muscle cells
keep part of what they built as a form
of memory. It has been shown in animals
. In humans, it is still being debated.
But anyone who has returned to lifting
after a break knows it. It comes back
fast. And that is where the real
advantage of muscle lies. Not the 13
calories, but the reserve. Because
after age 30, if you do nothing, you
lose muscle a little every year without
even noticing. And it accelerates with
age. At 70, that muscle is what decides
if you climb the stairs alone, get back
up after a fall, or carry your
groceries. Your strength is your
insurance for later. But stamina has
its own card to play, too: the brain.
In a famous study, older adults walked
at a brisk pace three times a week for
1 year. A part of their brain used for
memory, the hippocampus, grew by about
2%. In those who only did stretching,
it continued to shrink as it does with
age. Endurance exercise nourishes the
brain. Weight training does too, for
that matter, but cardio has the
strongest evidence. So in the end,
which one lives longer? Large studies
provide a clear answer. Good stamina is
one of the best signs of a long life
that we know of. Strength too; stronger
people live longer on average. And in a
large analysis that grouped hundreds of
thousands of people, the lowest risk of
death was not among those who only did
cardio, nor those who only did weight
training. It was among those who did
both. Around 40%less risk. So the real
answer is a third guy. He also trains
three times a week, but in every
session, he does both. First, his
strength training: push-ups, pull-ups,
squats, until near failure, making the
exercise a little harder each time.
Then, 20 minutes of running or brisk
walking. Three sessions, not one more
than our two other guys. And no,
running will not make his muscles melt
away. At this level, for someone who
isn't training for a marathon, the two
mix very well. The only advice:
strength training first when you're
fresh, and running afterward. A year
later, he is stronger than the runner.
He has more stamina than the gym guy.
And if he has to stop for 3 months, his
strength holds up. And if you want the
strength training part ready to go with
week-by-week progression, I wrote the
cardio method: 10 programs from
beginner to advanced, nutrition, and
progression all with body weight. The
link is in the description. The gym guy
built a body, the runner built an
engine, the third one built both, and
he didn't do a single extra session.
Yeah.

In 2023, a man held a plank for 9 hours
and 38 minutes. As for you, I’m only
asking for one minute, just one, every
day for a year. And that minute will
change things in your body, not
necessarily the ones you think. There is
one area it protects that almost nobody
thinks about. Around the 3rd week, there
is a trap. If you fall into it, your
minute becomes useless. And we’re going
to talk about your abs. At the end, I’ll
tell you exactly what to add to this
minute so they really show. So, we’re
going to follow this minute day by day,
month by month. What changes, in what
order, and what no one tells you. Day 1
. You place your forearms on the floor,
elbows right under your shoulders. You
extend your legs. Your body forms a
straight line from head to heels and you
start the timer. 10 seconds. Easy. You
wonder why everyone makes such a big
deal out of it. 20 seconds. Your belly
starts to heat up. 30 seconds. And now,
it starts to shake. Not just a little.
Your whole body vibrates, like a washing
machine on the spin cycle. It’s not that
you’re weak, your muscle fibers are
getting tired. So, your brain sends them
increasingly strong signals and calls
for reinforcements. But the
reinforcements don’t all arrive at the
same time. It holds in fits and starts.
That’s what the shaking is. 40 seconds.
Your shoulders are burning more than
your belly. Your hips start to sag and
your lower back arches. From this point
on, it’s not even your abs working
anymore, it’s your back taking the
strain. One minute. You collapse onto
the mat. Remember this minute well, it’s
your starting point. In a year, we’ll
compare it to what you’ve become. Day 2
. You wake up and surprise, almost
nothing. Not the heavy soreness of your
first push-ups or your first squats.
Soreness comes mostly from moments where
the muscle slows down while lengthening
, like when you lower yourself in a
push-up. In the plank, nothing lengthens
. Everything stays static. That’s why
you can do it again the very next day
and the day after that. Week 2. You can
now hold your minute without collapsing
. And when you look at your belly in the
mirror, nothing has changed. Normal.
What changed isn't the muscle, it's the
control.
Your brain has learned to switch on the
front, side, and deep stomach muscles
all at once, like a belt you suddenly
tighten. The muscle is the same; it's
just better controlled.
Week 3, the trap. Your minute has become
easy, so you do what everyone else does
. You move up to a minute and a half,
then two minutes, then three. You see
challenges go by—five-minute planks, ten
minutes—and you tell yourself the longer
it is, the more effective it is.
Remember the man who held it for 9 hours
and 38 minutes. He has incredibly
enduring abs, for sure. But you, you
don't need to hold it for 9 hours. In
real life, your stomach never works for
9 hours straight. It works hard for a
few seconds when you lift a box, when
you carry a heavy bag in one hand, or
when you catch yourself from slipping.
Beyond a minute of an easy plank, you're
no longer really training your strength
; you're mostly training your patience.
There is a Canadian researcher who spent
his career studying the back, Stuart
McGill. He advises the opposite of these
challenges: not a long, soft hold, but
10-second holds, done at full intensity
. In a study from his lab, young men did
sets of 10-second holds for 6 weeks.
This group gained the most core
stiffness, more than the group that did
moving exercises—the kind of bracing
that makes you solid when you push, pull
, or carry. So, keep your minute, but
break it up: 6 times 10 seconds. And
during those 10 seconds, tighten
everything as if someone were about to
punch you in the gut: glutes squeezed,
pelvis slightly tucked, as if you want
to pull your belt toward your chin, with
your elbows pushing into the floor. 10
seconds like that, and you'll be shaking
harder than during your entire first
minute. And when that also becomes easy
, move your elbows further forward, in
front of your head. The further your
supports are, the longer the lever, and
the harder your stomach has to work.
Researchers have measured it: a plank
with elbows far forward and the pelvis
tucked works the abs much harder than a
classic plank; it's still a minute, but
a minute that actually works. First
month, you lift your T-shirt in the
mirror; your belly hasn't melted away.
And I have to be honest with you, it's
not the plank that's going to make it
melt. Researchers had a group of people
do ab exercises five days a week for six
weeks. Seven different exercises, just
for the stomach. They ate just as they
had before. After six weeks, their abs
had much more endurance, but their belly
fat hadn't changed at all, neither on
the scale nor in their waistline. Your
body doesn't just pull fat from right
above the muscle that's working.
But don't give up on your minute yet,
because fat is only half the story. Your
abs, the other half, we'll get to that
at the end. And in the meantime, your
minute is doing something much more
important.
Second month. In the 80s, in Denmark,
researchers measured hundreds of people
, among other things, how long they
could hold a position lying on their
stomach with their torso hanging in the
air, without moving. Then, they waited a
year. Among men who had never had back
pain, those who held the position for
the shortest time were more likely to
have back pain for the first time.
Finnish researchers repeated the test a
few years later. Those who lasted the
shortest time were about three times
more likely to have back pain within the
year. The place your minute protects is
your back. But look closely at which
muscles they measured: the ones in the
back, not the ones in the front. Your
plank, however, works mostly the front.
So, from now on, your minute is changing
form. 20 seconds of plank, 20 seconds on
the side—10 on each side, body perfectly
straight on one elbow—and 20 seconds
lying on your stomach, with arms and
legs off the ground. The front, the
sides, the back. Still just one minute.
Third month. You start to feel it
somewhere other than on the mat. You
carry your groceries with one hand and
your torso no longer leans to the side.
During push-ups, your body stays
straight until the last rep, instead of
collapsing in the middle. At the end of
the day, in front of the computer, you
sit a little straighter, without even
thinking about it. And there is an
effect that no one thinks about. A few
years ago, researchers gathered 270
studies on sports and blood pressure.
The type of training that lowered the
top number the most was neither running
nor cycling. It was exercises where you
hold still without moving. In the lead,
the wall sit.
The plank wasn't tested in these studies
, but it’s the same type of effort.
Hold, tighten, breathe.
Month four, and that's where it gets
dangerous. Not because it’s hard, but
because it’s become mundane. No more
shaking, no more novelty, and in the
mirror, nothing spectacular. One morning
, you skip your minute, then the next
day too, and your minute vanishes
without you ever really deciding to quit
. What makes the difference at that
moment isn't motivation, it's where
you've slotted that minute into your day
. Attach it to a moment that happens
every day, no matter what. Right before
your shower, or in the evening, when you
put your phone away to sleep. The moment
arrives, the minute comes with it. And
if you skip one, it's no tragedy. In a
British study on habits, missing a day
now and then changed almost nothing. A
simple rule: never two days in a row.
One missed day is an accident; two days
is the start of a new habit—the habit of
quitting. And be honest, a minute—you
don't even have time to come up with an
excuse. Six months. Do you remember your
minute of the day? The one where you
collapsed after? It feels like a long
time ago. Those 10 seconds that felt
miles away, the ones that made you shake
harder than anything, are now part of
your routine. By the way, do you know
why the U.S. Army included the plank in
its test? For decades, American soldiers
took a test involving 2 minutes of
nonstop sit-ups. Sit-ups were removed.
Since 2022, the core test is the plank,
and it remained in the new 2025 test.
According to the Army, the plank
measures core strength better. A soldier
doesn't do sit-ups in the field; they
carry, lift, and endure. To pass the
test, you have to hold the plank for
about 1 to 1.5 minutes, depending on age
and gender. On day one, you collapsed at
1 minute; you would have failed. Today,
you would pass it easily. One year, 365
minutes. That’s about 6 hours in the
year, not even the time the world record
holder held it in one go. And look at
what those 6 hours have changed. A back
that can take it, a core that stays firm
when you lift, carry, or push, cleaner
push-ups, a body that stays upright, and
a habit so ingrained it feels effortless
. Your Day 1 minute, the one that wiped
you out, is now just your warm-up. So,
what about abs? Here is what nobody
tells you. You already have the outline
of your six-pack. Everyone is born with
it. They are bands of tendons that cross
your abdominal muscle and divide it into
squares. But for that definition to show
, two things must meet, and most people
only work on one. One, a muscle thick
enough for the squares to pop out. A
flat muscle, even under very thin skin,
doesn't show much of anything. That’s
your minute, plus a few exercises where
your torso curls, like crunches or leg
raises. Two, a thinner layer on top. And
that is handled on your plate. No
extreme diet. A few less calories than
you burn, enough protein to keep your
muscle, and some patience. Do both at
the same time, and one morning, in front
of the mirror, your abs will appear. If
you want both ready-made, the training
and the nutrition, I wrote the Cardio
method. 10 programs from beginner to
advanced, week-by-week progression, and
bodyweight-only nutrition. The link is
in the description. And if you keep
going, in 5 or 10 years, you’ll be
carrying boxes, suitcases, maybe
children, and you’ll spend hours sitting
. And your minute will be one of the
reasons your back can keep up. Let’s
recap. Day 1, you’re shaking. Week 3,
you make your minute harder instead of
making it longer. Month 2, it protects
your back. Month 4, you don’t let it go
. And for abs, the minute underneath,
the plate on top. The world record
holder lasted 9 hours and 38 minutes,
once. You, you’re going to last one
minute, 365 times.

subtitles.plaintext:
Your arms look decent from the side,
but as soon as you face forward, they
disappear. Yet, you've been doing
push-ups for months, maybe even
pull-ups. The problem isn't your effort
; it’s that your arm isn't one muscle
, it’s three, and you're likely only
working one. For an arm to look big, it
needs three things. Width, height, and
depth. Each one depends on a different
muscle. I’ll give you a home exercise
for each one without dumbbells. And pay
close attention to the third part. It
makes up almost two-thirds of your arm.
Part one, width. If your arm looks thin
from the front, it’s width you're
missing. And the muscle responsible,
which almost no one knows, is the
brachialis. It’s hidden under your
biceps and sticks out on the sides of
the arm. When it grows, it pushes your
biceps up and your arm widens,
especially seen from the front. To work
it, use the hammer curl. It’s a
normal curl but with palms facing each
other as if you were holding a hammer.
This grip takes some work away from the
biceps and gives more to the brachialis
. No dumbbells? Grab two shopping bags,
fill them with water bottles, and hold
them by the handles. Elbows glued to
your sides. Bring them up, squeeze for
a second at the top, and lower them
slowly over 3 seconds. Don't just drop
the weight. The lowering phase is half
the work. Three sets of 12 to 15. And
at the end of each set, your arm should
really be burning. If not, add another
bottle. Part 2. Height. This is the
muscle everyone knows: the biceps.
It’s what creates the peak when you
flex your arm. And I have good news:
with bodyweight, you have something
better than the curl. The supinated
pull-up, with palms facing toward you.
In this grip, your biceps must bend the
elbow and pull your entire body weight.
Researchers have measured its activity.
Palm facing you, it works harder than
palm facing away. The detail that
changes everything: go all the way down
, arms fully extended every rep. It’s
at the bottom, when the biceps is
stretched, that it works the hardest. A
half pull-up means a half-bicep. Can't
do a pull-up yet? Do Australian
pull-ups on a low bar, palms facing you
, or negatives. Get to the top with a
stool and lower yourself as slowly as
possible. Three sets until one or two
reps from failure. Part 3. The most
important depth comes from the muscle
at the back of your arm, the triceps.
It makes up nearly two-thirds of your
arm volume. If your arm looks flat,
that's why. And the triceps has a
secret: it has three parts. The largest
one, the long head, is the only one
that crosses your shoulder. It is only
truly stretched when your arm is raised
above your head. Push-ups and dips,
with arms by your sides, almost never
work it. A 2023 study confirmed this.
For 12 weeks, one group did overhead
extensions, the other did them with
arms by their sides. With the same
effort, the first group's triceps grew
about 40%more, and the long head about
50%more. So, the exercise: the overhead
extension with a backpack. Fill it with
books, hold it with both hands, arms
extended above your head, then bend
your elbows and lower the bag behind
your neck as low as possible. You
should feel the back of your arm
stretching. Come back up by extending
your arms. Only your forearms should
move. Your elbows should stay pointed
toward the ceiling. Three sets of 10 to
15. Go slowly, especially at the bottom
. Specifically, the workout. Twice a
week, for example, Tuesday and Saturday
. Three sets of chin-ups when you are
fresh. Three sets of backpack
extensions. Three sets of hammer curls.
2 minutes of rest between sets. 20
minutes and you're done. And for your
arms to really grow, one single rule.
Record your repetitions. At each
session, try to do one more than the
time before. When you reach 15 clean
repetitions, make the exercise harder.
One more bottle in the bags, one more
book in the backpack. Without that,
your body has no reason to change. The
arm is a small muscle; it grows slowly.
Eat enough protein, around 1g per kilo
of body weight per day, sleep 7 to 9
hours, and count on 6 to 8 weeks before
seeing a real difference. And if you
want all of this ready-made with
week-by-week progression, I wrote the "
Method Cardio" with 10 programs from
beginner to advanced, covering
nutrition and progression, all using
body weight. The link is in the
description. Thin arms are not a life
sentence. They are just two muscles you
had forgotten. Yeah.
